# APPENDIX BB

### DEFINITION OF A DEPENDENT CHILD

### Effective October 24, 2017, the definition of a “dependent child" is:

### A dependent child, in respect of a parent, is a child who:

### a. has one of the following relationships with the parent:

i. is the biological child of the parent, if the child has not been adopted by a person other than the spouse or common-law partner of the parent ii.is the adopted child of the parent
### b. is in one of the following situations of dependency:

i.is less than 22 years of age and is not a spouse or common-law partner ii.is 22 years of age or older, has depended substantially on the financial support of the parent since before the age of 22 and is unable to be financially self-supporting due to a physical or mental condition
#### Former Definitions of a Dependent Child:

Between August 1, 2014, and October 23, 2017, the definition of "dependent

### child" was as follows:

A dependent child, in respect of a parent, is a child who

### a. has one of the following relationships with the parent:

i.is the biological child of the parent, if the child has not been adopted by a person other than the spouse or common-law partner of the parent
### ii.is the adopted child of the parent

b. is in one of the following situations of dependency:
i.is less than 19 years of age and is not a spouse or common-law partner ii. is 19 years of age or older and has depended substantially on the financial support of the parent since before the age of 19 and is unable to be financially self-supporting due to a physical or mental condition For additional information refer to the following link:
[http://cicintranet.ci.gc.ca/connexion/tools-outils/perm/definitions-eng.aspx?letterNum=4](http://cicintranet.ci.gc.ca/connexion/tools-outils/perm/definitions-eng.aspx?letterNum=4)

# APPENDIX CC

### ADDING A DEPENDENT TO AN APPLICATION

Before adding a Dependent the RA MusT confirm that the dependent in question should be added to the application. The RA will verify what documents and/or fees must be requested and received

### There are two ways to receive a request to Add a Dependent/Spouse/Common-Law Partner

# (DEP/SP/CL).

R10 in Progress-The client submits a request to add a DEP/SP/CL via Client Enquiry. R10 Complete-File is forwarded to a Program Assistant via email from the team leader.

CLIENT REQUESTS TO ADD A CANADIAN DEPENDENT

- If the client submits a request to add a DEP/SP/CLP and the individual is a Canadian Citizen adding the dependent is not required, as long as there is proof of Citizenship provided (Birth Certificate, Passport, PR card). For PR status citizens, refer to the RA, park the file, and await direction prior to proceeding, PR status must be verified.
- Note the following for requests with confirmed Canadian citizens at the bottom of EE note: Dependent not associated to application as [spouse/common-law partner/child] is a [Canadian Citizen OR Permanent Resident of Canada]. Proof of status provided.
ADDING A DEPENDENT- R10 IN PROGRESS

- If the application in progress contains Client Information or a Client Enquiry that requests to add a DEP/SP/CLP, make note of the DEP/SP/CLP to be added, and continue to review the remaining documents for R10 completeness. If the file is R10 incomplete
Proceed with rejection (See Appendix X) If the file is R10 complete Promote as per R10 processing procedures, do not add EE Eligibility note Park the file Refer to the RA for review and await direction. Once confirmation is received, add the DEP/SP/CLP follow the steps under Adding a Dependent R10 Complete When the documentation is received, fees allocated, and file is now R10 complete proceed to add in the EE Eligibility note, include the added

## DEP/SP/CLP in the note, ensure criminality is noted appropriately (see

Appendix F) Enter the following at the bottom of your EE Eligibility note: Spouse/CLP/Dep child added after ITA

## APPENDIX II

RECONSIDERATIONS

For all reconsideration requests, any information received after the decision has been made is not acceptable. Exceptions to this procedure may arise due to circumstances at the time. Each case should be examined in detail on an individual basis.

## Examples of Reconsideration Requests:

Example 1: You rejected the application for a missing FBI clearance. PA submits a reconsideration request advising proof the FBI clearance was applied for was provided with the original submission. When you review the file again, you realize you over looked the FBI clearance application and tracking info of application to FBI office in Clarksburg, West Virginia. This is considered best efforts and the file should have moved forward in processing, not rejected. Since an error was made in processing, you must reopen the file if R10 is passed. NOTE: If something else is missing and R10 is incomplete, file will not be reopened. Discuss with your TL prior to sending updated rejection letter.

Example 2: You rejected the application as the PC on file was issued before the client's last date of residence in that country. PA submits a reconsideration request with a newer version of the police certificate and advises they made a mistake in uploading and forgot to include the new version of the police certificate. Decision remains in this case, no error was made during processing on the department's behalf and PA submitted an application that was R10 incomplete.

In some cases, notification of a reconsideration request is received via email from CSU.

CSU Procedures:

Upload the email request to the application Receive the reconsideration request when they run the Provided Report. Notify the Program Assistant by email of the reconsideration request. Forward a template response to the client (Edit template to request applicant monitor their IRCC secure account for further information).

Applications containing French Correspondence requiring additional review will be charged to this code. A bilingual Agent will review the correspondence and forward the application accordingly. # Appendix LL

PASSPORTS AND TRAVEL DOCUMENTS

Clients are required to provide a valid passport or travel document for travel to Canada. A passport or travel document is considered valid if it's:

- legal not expired, and accepted by us (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada)
The following documents are not acceptable (by IRCC) as travel documents to Canada as they are considered unreliable and are NOT valid for travel to Canada:

Documents we don't accept (unreliable travel documents) The following documents are considered unreliable and are not valid for travel to Canada:

- Any Passport Issued by Somalia
- Non-machine readable passports issued by the Czech Republic
- Temporary passports issued by the Republic of South Africa
- Provisional passports issued by Venezuela
Please be advised, effective immediately if these unreliable documents are provided as travel documents on an application, the application is a REJECTION, the file is incomplete as the applicant has not provided a valid passport/travel document. They are not accepted by IRCC. The Program Assistant will insert into the REJECTION Letter the following link to the public information page, so the applicant can see the acceptable/unacceptable documents. Public information page below: [https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/passport-travel-document.html](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/passport-travel-document.html)

Occasionally there is a variation of the name in the VIZ section of the passport, or they have French accents or accent marks included over the letters. In these instances you must consult the Names Policy. FRENCH ACCENTS OR ACCENT MARKS:

If a client has specified a French accent in his/her name, and it is supported by the VIZ of their passport, the name must be recorded in GCMS as the primary name (these will not show in the MRZ).

If a client has specified a French accent in his/her name, and it is NOT supported by the VIZ of their passport (ex: in a document, or letter, etc), it will be recorded as an AKA in GCMS and the primary name will be recorded as per the MRZ.

The names found in the original language should never be recorded as part of the primary name or printed on citizenship and immigration documents, unless they contain French accents, in which case they are recorded in IRCC's system of record and on IRCC issued documents. Where possible, these names will be recorded as an "AKA" (alias) or "other name" in IRCC's system of record, for verification purposes.

GCMS accepts the following French accents: À-À - É-Ê - Ë - È - 1 - Î - Ô - Ü - ù - 0 - Ç.

## MEDICAL NOTES

•Client provides an expired medical, and it is added to the medical tracker. When completing the final note it is important to add the following below the medical line in your final R10 note: Email sent to CiO Sydney Medical for possible medical extension

Example – Medical was expired for both the PA and SP on the file, the note only needs to be added once:

Primary Applicant Medical Attached to UCI: Yes Spouse Medical Attached to UCI: Yes Email sent to CiO Sydney Medical for possible medical extension

Client provides a letter they need a medical, or don't have to provide one up front, or they provide a blank document as per the client information website. You will request the medical following the steps in Appendix MM. In the ADMM you will Toggle NO under the promo tab, Client Medical section. The following note must be added to your final R10 note: Medical Report Form Requested

Example – Medical was requested for the whole family, the note only needs to be added once:

Primary Applicant Medical Attached to UCI: No Spouse Medical Attached to UCI: No Medical Report Form Requested

- There may be instances where both situations for medicals apply, one individual has an expired medical, the others on file require a request. The example would be similar to the below in this case the PA had an expired medical, and the spouse required a request: Primary Applicant Medical Attached to UCI: Yes Spouse Medical Attached to UCI: No Email sent to CiO Sydney Medical for possible medical extension Medical Report Form Requested

## NOTES REVIEW QUESTIONS

Each note requires editing prior to being entered in GCMS. The following indicates what items should be included in your note, ask yourself the following questions when doing the review of your note: •Review Type: Is this filled in as Program Assistant?

- Application #: Make sure this is included and matches the file you will be processing
- Regulation: (LINE OF BUSINESS OF THE FILE)
- Min Score: (# pulls from GCMS EE Eligibility tab)
- Existing UCl or New UCl(s)
- Are there Stat Questions on this file, they should be noted here, and who they are for, PA or SP •Is there a representative/Designated Individual on this file or included with this file?
- Are medicals attached?
- Are the medicals expired? Did you include the correct extra note?
- - AND/OR-Were Medicals requested? (appendix MM) Did you include the correct extra note?
- Are fees verified?
- Language test results must be noted for PA, if provided by the SP they must be noted for the SP
- Education must be noted for PA, for Foreign Credential it must be noted EXACTLY as the ECA. Foreign credential must be noted if it is provided or not.
- Canadian education noted? Is it undeterminable? Did you include the edoc#?
- Is there a SP? If so, their education must be noted as well
- Police certificates must be noted if they are provided whether they are required or not. Refer to the notes section of this manual for guidance, if there are stat questions on this file, the recommendation must be changed to review required
- Did you add the Pending Biometrics RCMP results note as required? •Is the AGE listed? •Was there any documents set for review such as Client Information or a Client enquiry?
- Did you have any additional notes on the side bar of your ADMM to address before finalizing your note. TIP: ALWAYS review your note prior to adding it to the GCMS Notes tab. Ensure all necessary changes are made and any additional details are added as required.

Some rejection reasons regarding Police Certificates and Education are already included in the Rejection Letter Template. ## Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

Canadian immigration and refugee law concerns the area of law related to the admission of foreign nationals* into Canada, their rights and responsibilities once admitted, and the conditions of their removal. The primary law on these matters is the "Immigration and Refugee Protection Act"(IRPA).

“foreign national" means a person who is not a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident and includes a stateless person. A foreign national may be outside Canada or already in Canada.

“permanent resident" of Canada refers to a person who has acquired resident status under IRPA, and not subsequently lost that status.

The "Immigration and Refugee Protection Act"(IRPA) is an Act of the Parliament of Canada, passed in 2002, and is the primary federal legislation regulating immigration to Canada. It replaced the "Immigration Act" of

1976. How to read IRPA The legislation is composed of two main parts: The Act and The Regulations. Throughout this manual, references to “the Act" include regulations made under it as well. IRPA creates a high level framework detailing the goals and guidelines the Canadian government has set with regard to immigration into Canada by foreign residents. The Regulations contain the laws created to fit within the IRPA in order to specify how the IRPA is to be applied. Sections of IRPA are commonly preceded by an “A” (ie. A12), whereas sections of the Regulations are commonly preceded by an “R” (ie. R70).

- to permit Canada to pursue the maximum social, cultural and economic benefits of immigration;
- to see that families are reunited in Canada;
- to protect public health and safety and to maintain the security of Canadian society;
- to promote international justice and security by fostering respect for human rights and by denying access to Canadian territory to persons who are criminals or security risks; and
- to offer safe haven to persons with a well-founded fear of persecution based on race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group, as well as those at risk of torture or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment;

This Act is to be applied in a manner that:

(a) furthers the domestic and international interests of Canada;
(b) promotes accountability and transparency by enhancing public awareness of immigration and refugee programs;
(c) facilitates cooperation between the Government of Canada, provincial governments, foreign states, international organizations and non-governmental organizations;
(d) ensures that decisions taken under this Act are consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, including its principles of equality and freedom from discrimination and of the equality of English and French as the official languages of Canada;
(e) supports the commitment of the Government of Canada to enhance the vitality of the English and French linguistic minority communities in Canada; and

(f) complies with international human rights instruments to which Canada is signatory.

### Permanent Residents

IRPA provides the rules by which a foreign national can be deemed inadmissible or denied entry to Canada; be admitted to Canada on a temporary basis; obtain status in Canada as a Permanent Resident; maintain their status in Canada; and more. The following section highlights some important sections of the act and regulations.

## Requirements Before Entering Canada

A11. (1) A foreign national must, before entering Canada, apply to an officer for a visa or for any other document required by the regulations. The visa or document may be issued if, following an examination, the officer is satisfied that the foreign national is not inadmissible and meets the requirements of this Act.

A16. (1) A person who makes an application must answer truthfully all questions put to them for the purpose of the examination and must produce a visa and all relevant evidence and documents that the officer reasonably requires.

A18. (1) Every person seeking to enter Canada must appear for an examination to determine whether that person has a right to enter Canada or is or may become authorized to enter and remain in Canada.

Upon Entry A20. (1) Every foreign national who seeks to enter or remain in Canada must establish,

(a) to become a permanent resident, that they hold the visa or other document required under the regulations and have come to Canada in order to establish permanent residence; and
(b) to become a temporary resident, that they hold the visa or other document required under the regulations and will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay
A21. (1) A foreign national becomes a permanent resident if an officer is satisfied that the foreign national has applied for that status, has met the obligations set out in paragraph 20(1)(a) and subsection 20(2) and is not inadmissible.

Dual intent

(2) An intention by a foreign national to become a permanent resident does not preclude them from becoming a temporary resident if the officer is satisfied that they will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay. Right of permanent residents A27. (1) A permanent resident of Canada has the right to enter and remain in Canada, subject to the provisions of this Act. A28. (1) A permanent resident must comply with a residency obligation with respect to every five-year period.

## Economic Class

A12(2) A foreign national may be selected as a member of the economic class on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada.

One of the three Classes of immigration and permanent residence is the Economic Class, which includes applicants who will be assessed on the skills and/or expertise they could bring to Canada. The economic permanent resident applicants are assessed against a selection system based on a category. These categories are:

- Federal skilled worker
- Provincial nominee
- Canadian Experience
- Federal Skilled Trades
#### Federal Skilled Worker (FSW)

This program is designed for applicants who are skilled workers, who may become permanent residents on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada, and who intend to reside in a province other than Quebec. Successful applicants must have a minimum of one year of “skilled" work experience and meet the minimum requirements for education, language abilities as well as other requirements to

### demonstrate their ability to successfully establish themselves in Canada.

#### Provincial nominee (PNP)

Another type of independent permanent resident applicant is a provincial nominee. Applicants under this category are selected in consultation with the province interested in making the nomination. In some cases

### provinces will seek to nominate applicants with experience in occupations considered “in demand” within that

province. Applicants holding a provincial nomination must also meet federal requirements for admissibility.

#### Canadian Experience (CEC)

The Canadian Experience Class is prescribed as a class of persons who may become permanent residents on the basis of their Canadian experience and who:

- intend to reside in a province or territory other than Quebec; have acquired a minimum of one year work experience in Canada; have maintained temporary resident status during their qualifying period of work experience in Canada; and
- meet the language requirement.

and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada Information disclosed under the Access to Information Act L'information divulguée en vertu de la loi sur laccès à informalion Federal Skilled Trades (FST)

The Federal Skilled Trades Program is for people who want to become permanent residents based on being qualified in a skilled trade.

To apply, you must have work experience in a specific skilled trade and meet several other requirements.

Intent to reside

Applicants will indicate within their Express Entry application where they intend to reside when they become a permanent resident. Applicants who indicate an intention to reside in the province of Quebec are not eligible to apply under the CEC program. If you have concerns about the applicant's intention to reside in a province other than Quebec, the file should be referred to an officer for review. Keep in mind that an applicant's experience (either prior or current) in a province does not necessarily denote an intention to live there in the future.

## The Process

Economic Class applications for permanent residence are submitted to the Centralized Intake Office at CPC-Sydney in Nova Scotia. The CiO checks the application for completeness, creates the application in the electronic database, and process the payment. Decision making responsibility is shared between the three networks. Applications are transferred to other offices in the Domestic, International or Centralized Network for continued processing. In some cases CiO retains responsibility for the application up to final decision. Triage criteria have been developed to determine which applications are referred to which offices, and at which stage of processing the referral will take place.

After meeting specific eligibility criteria for the particular program as described above, all applicants still need to be admissible in order to be granted the status of Permanent Resident. Generally this would include a medical screening and background checks for criminality and security. Once all members of the family meet all requirements, each individual is issued a permanent resident visa that is processed when they arrive in Canada.

There are several Economic Class programs which are eligible for processing under EE, including: Federal Skilled Workers, Canadian Experience Class, Federal Skilled Trades, and certain Provincial Nominees.

Section 11.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) includes a new authority that supports the Express Entry system, and adds a new level of decision making for permanent residence applications. Under A11.2, we are able to refuse an EE application when the applicant does not meet minimum entry criteria (MEC) or did not or does not possess the qualifications for which they received their invitation to apply.

The 11.2 decisions for Canadian Experience Class applications will be the focus of this training. In the next module you will be introduced to some key concepts related to the Express Entry application management system, and look at both the requirement to maintain the MEC, and the requirement to prove and maintain the self-declared qualifications for which they were awarded points resulting in the invitation to apply.

## Introduction to Express Entry

Express Entry is an application management system. It is a method of ranking potential immigration candidates, choosing those with the highest qualifications and inviting them to apply for permanent residence. Candidates, or potential applicants, get the benefit of more efficient processing and accelerated processing times. For IRCC, it is a way for our department to better manage the intake of economic class applications and prevent backlogs (at least at the intake stage), while providing consistent, efficient processing for applicants.

Candidates create an online Express Entry profile in their MyCIC account and, if invited to apply, submit their application for permanent residence (APR) through their MyCIC account.

Express Entry POOL

Application Express Entry1 – MINIMUM ENTRY CRITERIA 2 – COMPREHENSIVE Submission AND POINTS SCORE RANKING SYSTEM3 - INVITATION TO APPLYfor permanent residence

Business Process

Foreign nationals who are interested in living in Canada permanently and who have work experience in a skilled occupation, may register and create a personal secure online account in with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada. During this process, potential applicants (Candidates) will enter information related to their: Age Level of education Language abilities Work experience Family members Details related to any job offers in Canada

The system will determine whether the foreign national meets the Minimum Entry Criteria (MEC) for any of the eligible programs for Express Entry processing, and assign a value to each applicable aspect according to the MEC.

When a candidate's profile shows that they meet the minimum entry criteria (MEC), the system automatically enters their profile into the Express Entry pool. Potential candidates MUST meet the criteria for one of the programs set up for EE in order to get into the pool.

Candidates receive a notification letting them know when their profile has been placed in the EE pool, and that their profile will remain in the pool for 365 days. This notification gives the candidate their score and ranking

While in the pool, the candidate may update their profile at any time.

The message also gives them their Express Entry profile number and a Job Seeker validation code, which are automatically generated by the system. Candidates need their Job Seeker validation code to register for the Government of Canada's Job Bank, an electronic listing of jobs provided by employers from across Canada. Candidates without a job offer or a provincial or territorial nomination will be required to register with the Job Bank to complete and submit their Express Entry profile. Express Entry candidates can be matched with Canadian employers and jobs based on their skills, knowledge and experience.

At this point, the candidate is eligible to receive an Invitation to Apply (ITA) for the program whose requirements they appear to meet. A specific number of invitations are issued (ITA) on a regular, usually bi- weekly basis, to Express Entry candidates who have the highest Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) scores at the time of an Express Entry round of invitations. Those who receive an ITA have 60 days to apply. This deadline is indicated in the client's correspondence, which they can access in their MyCiC account. Candidates who are issued an ITA have three options: they can respond to the ITA; they can ignore it (in which case they are removed from the Express Entry pool); they can decline it, in which case they return to the pool for consideration in future rounds of invitations. Candidates may ONLY apply for permanent residence online if they receive an invitation to apply through the Express Entry system. Completing an online Express Entry profile or entering the pool doesn't guarantee that a candidate will be invited to apply for permanent residence.

A foreign national is considered to be a “CANDIDATE" up until he/she submits an application for permanent residence (APR). Once an application is submitted he/she is considered to be an “APPLICANT”.

The Comprehensive Ranking System, or CRS, is a points-based system used to assess and score a candidate's Express Entry profile and determine a candidate's position in the Express Entry pool. It ranks prospective skilled immigrants by looking at their skills, work experience, language ability, education and other factors that we know lead to success in Canada. Each candidate in the Express Entry pool is ranked according to points awarded for certain economic selection factors. A candidate's total score is known as the CRS score.

According to A10.3(1) and A87.3(3), the minister may give instructions with respect to the way immigration applications are processed. From time to time such Ministerial Instructions are released to guide our processing, and these instructions should be applied in conjunction with IRPA.

The Express Entry application management system is primarily governed using Ministerial Instructions. Throughout the training we will refer to the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system. We use these Ministerial Instructions to guide us in our decision making, specifically the decisions we make related to A11.2. Further decisions related to program eligibility and inadmissibility require the application of program regulations and other specific sections of IRPA.

As required by IRPA, subsection 10.3(4), all Ministerial Instructions related to Express Entry must be published on IRCC's website. Some Ministerial Instructions must also be posted in the Canada Gazette. The Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system came into force on January 1, 2015. The current and most recent version of the Express Entry MI's was released on June 26, 2018. The entire package of Ministerial Instructions has been posted in the Canada Gazette and on IRCC's website.

CRS points and the Ministerial Instructions

Intake: Receiving an Application for Permanent Residence submitted via Express Entry

Applicants are required to submit a complete electronic application for permanent residence (e-APR) within 60 calendar days of being issued an invitation to apply (ITA). The application and all supporting documents must be submitted electronically through the applicant's online account.

Applications are assessed for completeness up front at the ClO. An application found to be incomplete is rejected as per Section 10 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, and all fees associated with the application should be refunded to the applicant.

The Express Entry six-month processing standard begins when an application is assessed as complete and is promoted in the Global Case Management System (GCMS). It ends when Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) makes a final decision on the application.

A complete application must include the cost recovery fees and all supporting documentation to validate information contained in the applicant's Express Entry profile and e-APR.

Applicants and their family members must undergo upfront medical examinations and submit all required police certificates as part of their complete application. Medical results must be valid and applicants are encouraged to undergo medical examinations closer to the date their application is submitted to avoid processing delays.

A personalized document checklist is produced for each applicant when they submit their e-APR through their online account. The personalized checklist identifies the specific supporting documents required from each family member included on the application.

## Mandatory documents for all applicants

The following documents are mandatory and must be provided by all applicants.

Applications that do not contain the following documents are rejected as incomplete, and fees are refunded accordingly.

- Medical examination confirmation-for all family members, whether accompanying or not (Temporary Public Policy currently in effect, review current process)
- Police certificates – for the principal applicant and all family members 18 years of age or older, whether accompanying or not
- Copy of the biographical data page of a passport or travel document – required for all
- Proof of work experience – for the PA only

A11.2 Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

Visa or other document not to be issued

11.2 (1) An officer may not issue a visa or other document in respect of an application for permanent
residence to a foreign national who was issued an invitation to make that application if — at the time the invitation was issued or at the time the officer received their application — the foreign national did not meet the criteria set out in an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(e) or did not have the qualifications on the basis of which they were ranked under an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(h) and were issued the invitation.

Exceptions

(2) Despite subsection (1), an officer may issue the visa or other document if, at the time the officer received their application,
(a) the foreign national did not meet the criteria set out in an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(e) — or did not have the qualifications on the basis of which they were ranked under an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(h) — because the applicant's birthday occurred after the invitation was issued; or
(b) the foreign national did not have the qualifications they had at the time the invitation was issued and on the basis of which they were ranked under an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(h), but
- (i) they met the criteria set out in an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(e), and
- (ii) they occupied a rank that is not lower than the rank that a foreign national was required to have occupied to be invited to make an application.
According to A11.2 when reviewing an application, processing offices must determine if:

- the applicant possesses the qualifications that they declared in their e-APR, as corroborated by the applicant's supporting documentation; and the information provided in their Express Entry profile at the time of application, has not materially changed to the degree that the applicant would not have been issued an ITA in that round of invitations.
Processing offices must compare the information in the applicant's profile at the time of the round of invitations to the information in their e-APR to ensure that the applicant meets the requirements of section A11.2. Note that not all discrepancies should result in a refusal [A11.2(2)].

### Requirement to maintain the MEC

A11.2 specifies that applicants must meet the criteria set out in A10.3(e) to be accepted into the Express Entry pool and must also meet this criteria when they are issued an ITA and when they submit their e-APR.

10.3 (1) The Minister may give instructions governing any matter relating to the application of this Division, including instructions respecting (e) the criteria that a foreign national must meet to be eligible to be invited to make an application; The criteria referred to in this subsection is otherwise known as the “Minimum Entry Criteria" for the program in which the applicant is applying. Ministerial Instructions for Express Entry list the Minimum Entry Criteria (MEC) for each program (s.2 and s.5). If you determine that the applicant did not meet the MEC for the program at the time he/she was invited to apply, the application should be refused. If an applicant's situation changes in the time between when they receive an ITA and when they submit their e-APR to such a degree that they no longer meet the MEC, the application must be refused under section A11.2. An officer will need to consider whether the application should be refused for not meeting the minimum requirements of the federal program to which they are applying, or for misrepresentation (A40).
### Requirement to maintain the CRS score

A11.2 also specifies that an applicant must have the qualifications described in 10.3(1)(h) of IRPA at the time they are issued the invitation to apply and at the time the application is received.

10.3 (1) The Minister may give instructions governing any matter relating to the application of this Division, including instructions respecting (h) the basis on which an eligible foreign national may be ranked relative to other eligible foreign nationals The name of the system or basis on which EE candidates are ranked is the “Comprehensive Ranking System". Candidates are awarded a score for each of their self-declared qualifications. These scores are totaled and amount to the candidate's CRS score. When a round of invitations occurs, IRCC invites the top-ranked candidates in the Express Entry pool to apply for permanent residence. After each round of invitations, IRCC publishes the score of the lowest-ranked candidate to receive an ITA in that round of invitations. An applicant's CRS score is automatically recorded in GCMS at the time when
- their ITA is issued; and
- their e-APR is submitted.
Applicants are required to maintain the qualifications that led them to be included in the top-ranked candidates to be issued an ITA in a particular round of invitations. At the time of the e-APR, processing officers should compare both CRS scores to determine which of the following scenarios should be applied:

- If the applicant's CRS score at the time of the e-APR is equal to or higher than the lowest-ranked score in the round of invitations, the application will not be refused under section A11.2, as long as the applicant's supporting documentation corroborates their claims and they continue to meet the MEC for Express Entry, including the requirements of the program to which they were invited to apply.

- If the applicant's CRS score at the time of the e-APR is lower than the lowest-ranked score in the round of invitations, the application should be refused under section A11.2 for not having maintained the qualifications that would justify the ITA. The main exception to this is those applicants who lost points because they had a birthday between ITA and the submission of their e-APR – see the example scenario below.

Ministerial Instructions related to the CRS are revised periodically. Applications must be assessed under section A11.2 according to the Ministerial Instructions in force during the round of invitations to which the candidate is invited. In other words, an applicant's CRS score at the time of the ITA and at the time of application should be calculated based on the Ministerial Instructions in place at the time of the ITA.

Exemption to section A11.2(1): candidates whose birthday occurs after they receive an ITA

An applicant may have a birthday after they receive an ITA but before they submit their e-APR. Their change in age may lower their CRS score below the lowest score in the round of invitations, resulting in a refusal based on section A11.2.

When a change in age results in having the recalculated CRS points score fall below the lowest points score in that round of invitations, processing offices will apply the exemption in A11.2(2).

Example scenario: candidate has a birthday between ITA and e-APR

Jan is 35 years old when she receives her ITA. She has met the MEC for CEC and CRS points are above the minimum cut-off score at ITA. Between her ITA and e-APR, Jan turns 36. Due to her change in age, Jan's CRS score drops by 5 points, putting her below the lowest-ranked candidate in her round of invitations.

You will grant Jan the exemption and, consequently, Jan continues to meet the MEC/CRS score for A11.2. This exempts Jan from being refused under section A11.2 for her adjusted CRS score and for not meeting program requirements.

## Examining the CEC Minimum Entry Criteria

IRPA defines the classes in which foreign nationals can apply to immigrate to Canada, and requirements for each class and category/program within a class (program eligibility); selection factors that influence the

# individual's ability to become economically established (Selection); and grounds for inadmissibility to Canada

All programs included in Express Entry fall under the Economic Class. The Economic Class is generally prescribed as a class of persons who are skilled workers, who may become permanent residents on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada. Ministerial Instructions for Express Entry (s.2)

# defer to the specific sections of IRPR, for program criteria for each federal program:

- the Canadian experience class referred to in subsection 87.1(1) of the Regulations;
The Canadian Experience Class is for applicants who intend to reside in a province other than Quebec, and who have gained work experience IN CANADA in an occupation at the TEER 0, 1, 2 or 3. The Minimum Entry Criteria (MEC) required for CEC are:

- Skilled work experience in Canada
- Temporary resident status during qualifying work period(s)
- Language ability

Trades class. The Ministerial Instructions defer to the regulations for the definition of who is a member of a class for each program.

## Introduction to the NOC and NOC Matrix

NOC

The National Occupational Classification (NOC) is the nationally accepted reference on occupations in Canada. It is used analyze and communicate information about occupations, and to understand the jobs found throughout Canada's labour market. The NOC is a standard that classifies and describes the occupations in the Canadian economy.

### NOC Matrix

The NOC Matrix provides an overview of the entire occupational classification structure for jobs in Canada, based on Skill Levels and Broad Occupational Categories or Types of occupations. Skill Levels are represented in the columns while the Skill Types are found in rows. Senior Management and other Managerial occupations are found in the first column of the chart, indicating the presence of management across all segments of the labour market.

The occupational categories are displayed in rows and are represented by numbers zero (0) to nine (9) while the skill levels are displayed in columns and are identified by TEER categories 0 to 5. Managerial occupations, which are considered as TEER 0 occupations, are found on the left-end side of the chart, indicating the

# presence of management across all segments of the labour market.

For most economic class programs the requirement is that the work must be in the TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3

### Skill Types / Occupational Categories

0 Management occupations 00 Senior management occupations

## 01-09 Middle management occupations in various fields

1 Business, finance and administration occupations 2 Natural and applied sciences and related occupations 3 Health occupations 4 Occupations in education, law and social, community and government services

## 5 Occupations in art, culture, recreation and sport

6 Sales and service occupations

TEER 0, 1 :Professional Occupations, Usually Requiring a University Education Always have “0” or “1” as the second digit. For TEER 0, 1, the first digit will identify the skill type.

Example: NOC 31102: General Practitioners and Family Physicians 1 as the second digit indicates TEER 1; 3 as the first digit indicates Heath Occupations (type).

Example: NOC 60020: Retail and wholesale trade managers 0 as the second digit indicates TEER O; 6 as the first digit indicates Sales and service occupations TEER 0 Legislative and senior management occupations: High Level of Responsibility With all other TEER 1, 2, 3 level occupations, you need to pay attention to the second digit to identify the skill level. For Senior Management occupations this rule changes. NOC codes at the senior management level will always begin with a “00”, so they are easily identified.

Example: NOC 00013: Senior managers-health, education, social and community services and membership organizations 00 indicates Senior Management Occupation (level)

TEER 2, 3 :Technical, Usually Require College Education/Apprenticeship Training Will have “2” or “3” as the second digit. For TEER 2, 3, as with TEER 0, 1, the first digit will identify the skill type.

## Reviewing the NOC website:

Each NOC description includes the following elements:

Lead Statement The lead statement provides a general description of the occupation and the boundaries of the unit group. It also indicates the kinds of industries, workplaces or establishments where the occupation is found. Applicants must have performed the actions in the lead statement in order to include the period of work experience in the stated NOC.

Example Titles Example titles are the occupational titles commonly found within the group. This list is an extraction of a more expansive listing of alphabetical job titles found in the NOC Index of Titles. The example titles may help to determine if the work experience is in the stated NOC.

Main Duties The main duties section describes the most significant duties of the occupations in the group. Depending on the Unit Group, it may include:

- a series of statements that can be applied to all occupations in the group;
- two or more sub-sets of occupations with statements that apply to each sub-set or component; and/or
- a series of brief statements that are linked to specific occupations, that, while similar enough to be in the same group, can be described separately.
Statements in Italics, at the end of this section, identify a specialization that may exist within the occupation.

Note that there are times when employment duties overlap from one unit group to another. An assessment of job duties must include consideration of the duties that are most important for the particular occupation. In many cases it is not enough to determine that half or more than half of the listed duties have been performed by the applicant. Duties are organized and listed according to significance to the job – most prominent or important duties are listed first. If the statement begins with “may perform", the duty is not critical to that occupation.

Employment Requirements Employment requirements are prerequisites generally needed to enter the occupation. Several types of requirements are listed: •type and level of education including specific subject matter if relevant, starting with the lowest possible requirement for entry into the occupation; specific training required, including apprenticeship, on-the-job or internal training;

# experience in a related occupation, especially for supervisory or managerial occupations;

licenses, certificates or affiliations; and/or other requirements not dependent on formal education, such as athletic abilities, artistic talent or presentation of a portfolio. While some occupations have very specific employment requirements, others have a wide range of acceptable requirements. The following terminology is used to indicate the level of the requirement: •"Is required" indicates a definite requirement.

## Qualifying Work Experience

"Status" and “authorization" are separate in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). Work included to meet the MEC for CEC must be authorized work, and it must be performed while the applicant has valid TR status. A foreign national may have TR status and not be authorized to work.

Definition of “work” [R2] "Work" is defined in the Regulations as an activity for which wages are paid or commission is earned, or that competes directly with activities of Canadian citizens or permanent residents in the Canadian labour market

# [R2].

### Authorized Work

Work may be authorized for foreign nationals in Canada either with a work permit, or through another

## regulatory authority. Work permits may be issued to either visa-required or visa-exempt foreign nationals.

Work permits may be employer-driven, based on a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA), or they may be LMIA-exempt. Some temporary residents may be authorized to work without a work permit in certain

# situations. Keep in mind that work experience gained through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits

while a full-time student and on-campus work permits, does not meet the requirements for CEC. Whether work is performed with or without a work permit, you must ensure both that the work period was authorized AND that the foreign national held temporary resident status at the time.

### Employee vs. self-employed

In determining whether an applicant under the CEC was an employee or a self-employed individual during

## their period of qualifying work experience in Canada, you should consider factors such as:

- the degree of the worker's control or autonomy in terms of how and when work is performed, and the method(s) used to do the work; whether the worker owns and/or provides tools and equipment to accomplish the work; the degree to which the worker has to perform the work personally and whether the worker has the option of subcontracting work or hiring others to help and assist with completing the work; the degree of financial risk assumed by the worker, including whether the worker is required to make any investment in order to complete the work or provide the service and whether the worker is free to make business decisions that affect his/her ability to realize a profit or incur a loss (as opposed to the opportunity to earn commissions or other productivity bonuses); and any other relevant factors, such as written contracts.

Additional details regarding each of the above factors, and indicators that can be used when determining whether an individual is an employee or self-employed, are available in the Employee or Self-employed? CRA guide.

Determination of the degree of control can be difficult when examining the employment of professionals such as engineers, physicians and information technology consultants. Given their expertise and specialized training, they may need little or no specific direction in their daily activities. When examining the factor of

control, it is necessary to focus on both the payer's control over the worker's daily activities, and the payer's influence over the worker. There are also certain occupations in which individuals may be either self-employed or in an employer-employee relationship depending on the specific circumstances of their employment. More information on the determination of a worker's employment status for a number of specific employment categories is available on the CRA website.

Generally speaking, consultants/contractors are considered to be self-employed individuals in a “contract for services” business relationship. For example, independent contractors in the financial, real estate and business service industries. Similarly, individuals who hold substantial ownership and/or exercise management control of a business for which they are also employed are generally considered to be self-employed.

Each application under the CEC is to be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. No one piece of evidence substantiating work experience is to be taken as “conclusive” evidence. The final decision as to the employment status of the applicant for the purposes of meeting CEC requirements rests with the officer at6 the time of assessment. If you have concerns that the applicant may be self-employed and you are unable to make a determination on your own, refer the file to program support.

Duration of Work: Calculation of One Year You must ensure work experience is acquired in Canada, through authorized employment by a third party. To determine whether the applicant has the requisite work experience, the main duties listed in the letters from the employer are assessed and compared against the information in the National Occupational Classification (Noc) website. However, the work experience assessment is not based on the Letters of Employment exclusively; the entire file, including employment letters and supporting documents, must be reviewed to satisfy you that the applicant has performed the actions described in the lead statement, and a substantial number of the main duties of the occupation. Note: the applicant's educational and personal history background may also be a factor in making a positive assessment of work experience. However, deficiencies in education and personal background should not be used to disqualify work experience claimed.

Applicants must have at least 12 months of full-time, Canadian skilled work experience (or the equivalent in part-time work experience) in one or more TEER 0, 1, 2 or 3 occupations within the 36 months before the date of application receipt [R87.1(2)(a)]. Full–time work experience means working at least 30 paid hours per week. Part-time work may be included as long as the applicant has gained the equivalent amount of experience as someone who worked full-time for at least one year (1560 hours).

Work experience does not need to be continuous to qualify, but the period of 12 months of required employment does not include any extended breaks in employment, periods of unemployment, prolonged sickness or parental leave. An allowance for a reasonable period of vacation time will generally be made in calculating the period of qualifying work experience (e.g., a two-week period of paid vacation leave within a given 52-week period in which the applicant was engaged in qualifying work experience). An allowance for normal vacation time during a period of qualifying work experience cannot be used as a substitute or proxy for meeting the in-Canada element of the work experience requirement (i.e. work experience obtained outside Canada will not be considered as though the applicant had been on a period of vacation in order to be counted as part of the period of in-Canada work experience). While officers will account for a reasonable period of vacation time in calculating the period of qualifying work experience in Canada, each application is

During the period of employment, an officer must be satisfied that the applicant “performed the actions described in the lead statement for the occupation(s); and “performed a substantial number of the main duties of the occupation(s)”. Any period of employment when the applicant was engaged in full-time study will not be included in calculating the period of qualifying work experience (ie. work through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits while a full-time student and on-campus work permits). Officers should verify the work permit information in GCMS to ensure there are no concerns.

Principal applicants are requested to provide documentary evidence of their work experience in Canada through a combination of: a copy of their most recent work permit (unless they are work-permit exempt), copies of their most recent T4 tax information slips and Notice of Assessment (NOA) issued by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) or a sufficient combination of other supporting documentation, and employer letters of reference for all periods of qualifying work experience claimed in the application.

Canadian employers are responsible for deducting and remitting Canada Pension Plan (CPP) contributions, Employment Insurance (El) premiums, and income tax from remuneration or other amounts they pay to their employees to the CRA. They must also provide employees with a record of their remuneration and deductions in the form of a T4 tax information slip. The T4 slip is therefore key documentary evidence for the vast majority of CEC applicants to demonstrate that they were in an employer-employee work relationship during their period of qualifying work experience in Canada.

However, there is no obligation under the regulations that CEC applicants provide a T4 tax information slip or NOA specifically with their application, and these particular documents cannot be considered conclusive evidence or the only evidence accepted for the purposes of substantiating whether an applicant has qualifying Canadian work experience. As such, in the absence of a T4 tax information slip or NOA, documents which may help substantiate the applicant's work experience in Canada could include a record or letter of employment from the Canadian employer, work contracts and pay stubs.

In all cases, the onus is on the applicant to establish that they meet the CEC program criteria at the time of their application. All applicants are required to provide satisfactory evidence of their work experience in Canada, including the fact that they were in an employer-employee relationship during their period of qualifying work experience.

### Work Permits

Conditions

## Work permits are always issued with conditions. For example, all temporary residents have an automatically

imposed condition that they must leave Canada at the end of their authorized period of stay. Specific conditions related to temporary work are imposed by an officer and are specific to the client's situation. It is important you understand the imposed conditions such as:

- a period of authorized stay the type of work the employer location of work times and period of work Period of authorized stay
A work permit will always indicate the period authorized for stay in Canada (ie. Expiry date). The authorized period of stay may be longer than the authorized period of work [R185(a) and R185(b)(iv)].

### Type of work

There are a variety of situations where the type of work/occupation is restricted. There are employer-specific work permits and also “open" employer work permits that are occupation-restricted [R185(b)(i)]. Employer-specific work permits are issued for foreign nationals to work in a specific occupation, for a specific employer. These work permits are employer-driven, where the employer must apply for and receive an LMIA* before the foreign national can apply for a work permit, or must issue an offer of employment for LMIA-exempt workers [R204-R208]. “Open" restricted work permit: Where the employer is not listed, a location and/or occupation may be restricted. An occupation may be restricted due to medical or program requirements. For example, the person may not be able to work in jobs where the protection of the public health is required, if they have been assessed as M2, M3, or M4. *LMIA: Labour Market Impact Assessment, or an assessment — provided to the officer by the Department of Employment and Social Development that the requirements set out in subsection 203(1) with respect to the offer have been met

### The employer

Work permits issued under R200(1)(c)(ii.1) will identify the employer. The employer name will match the employer named on the LMIA or the offer of employment. When an officer issues an employer-specific work permit under an LMIA exemption, GCMS will automatically insert the employer's name into the “Employer" field.

### Location of work

Location of work must be imposed as a condition where an LMlA has been issued or where it is a requirement of the LMIA exemption [R185(b)(iii)]. For example, when an employer has several franchise locations but indicates only one location on the offer of employment, the work permit should reflect the physical location of work and restrict the work to that Page |33

A-2025-58066-000346

Immigration, Refugees mmigration, Réfugiés et Citoyenneté Canada Information disclosed under the Accessto Information Act L'nformation divulguée en vertu de la toi sur l’accès à Tinformation location. However, if the employer indicates in the offer of employment that the worker will be working at multiple work locations, the officer should not restrict the work permit to a single location and should indicate in the “Remarks" field that the worker is authorized to work at the various locations across Canada. For LMlA- supported work permits, the location of work must match the destination on the LMIA. For LMIA-exempt work permits, if the location of work is important to the exemption (such as for provincial nominees), then the location will be specified and the restriction on location imposed.

Times and periods of work

While the period of authorized stay may extend beyond the authorization period of work, the period of work may never extend beyond the duration specified in the LMIA or offer of employment. There may also be conditions where worker is not authorized to work at specific times or dates. For example, seasonal agricultural workers are never to work between December 15 and January 1; students are automatically authorized to work for up to 20 hours per week in their off-campus employment during the semester.

Post-graduation work permit (PGWP): LMIA-exemption code C43 Post-graduation work permits are exempt from Labour Market Impact Assessments. They are considered “open” work permits, and are coded in GCMS as C43. With a post-graduation work permit, as with all open work permits, graduates can work full time, work part time, or be self-employed. A post-graduation work permit may be issued based on the length of the study program for a minimum of 8 months up to a maximum of 3 years. When determining the length of a post-graduation work permit, officers may consider the duration of the program of study in Canada. When assessing work performed while under a PGWP, officers should assess carefully to ensure that the NOC requirements are met, and that the applicant was not self-employed.

Bridging Work permit (BOWP): LMIA-exemption code A75 Requirements for a bridging open WP are: they are currently in Canada;

- they have valid status on a work permit that is due to expire in four months or less; they are the principal applicant on an application for permanent residence under FSW, CEC, FST, or PNP
- they have received a positive eligibility assessment on their permanent residence application under one of the Economic Class programs above (EE: passed A11.2 decision) they have applied for an open work permit; and they have paid the work permit processing fee and the Open Work Permit Holder fee For more information: [http://cicintranet.ci.gc.ca/connexion/tools-outils/temp/work-](http://cicintranet.ci.gc.ca/connexion/tools-outils/temp/work-) travail/prov/bridging-transitoires-eng.aspx Validity period for work permits
When determining the validity period of a work permit, officers must first consider the passport validity. A foreign national must hold a passport that is valid for the period authorized for their stay [R52(1)], unless the applicant is exempted (such as U.S. nationals). A work permit cannot be extended beyond the validity of the passport, as doing so would be putting the temporary worker in a position of non-compliance. [Exceptions to this are noted in subsection R52(2)].

Generally speaking, it is possible for work experienced gained under R186 and 187 to apply for CEC, as long as they meet program requirements (1 year in the past 3; NOC 0, A or B; maintain TR status while working). For example, Diplomats, consular officers and other foreign representatives and officials are authorized to work in Canada without a work permit [R186(b) and (c)]. However, there are exceptions to this and not all work authorized without permit is eligible for the CEC program. For example, R186(a) and R187– Business Visitors: Work experience obtained as a business visitor cannot be calculated for the Canadian experience class (CEC). Business visitors must not have an intent to enter the Canadian labour market (that is, they must have no gainful employment in Canada). Examples: attendance at business meetings, trade conventions or exhibitions; procurement of Canadian goods and services; people seeking entry to repair, service, set up, test or supervise work on specialized commercial or industrial equipment purchased or leased outside Canada; certain foreign nationals in the commercial production industry, such as advertising, or in the film or recording industry, including those using studios (limited to small groups that are renting studios and not entering the labour market).

## Temporary resident status

### Admission to Canada

In addition to meeting the eligibility requirements for the temporary resident category under which they have applied, applicants must be authorized to enter Canada – usually this means a foreign national must obtain either a visa or an electronic travel authorization (if they are visa-exempt), which will allow them to enter Canada. A temporary resident visa (TRV) is an official counterfoil document issued by a visa office that is placed in a person's passport to show that they have met the requirements for admission to Canada as a temporary resident. A TRV does not guarantee entry to Canada (ie. Does not give the “right" of entry), nor does it grant temporary resident status in Canada. The border services officer who examines the foreign national upon entry will determine the purpose and duration of the visit. A handwritten date below the stamp indicates the date by which the foreign national must leave Canada. It is at this point that the foreign national receives temporary resident status. A temporary resident who leaves Canada will no longer have temporary resident status.

### Status During Period(s) of Work

It is possible for work permits to be issued to those who may not have status as a temporary resident [R202] –

## ie. Refugee claimants who cannot support themselves without working. A CEC applicant must have held

temporary resident status during the period of work used to meet the CEC Minimum Entry Criteria. A foreign national has temporary resident status when they have been found to meet the requirements of the legislation to enter AND/OR remain in Canada as a visitor, student, worker or temporary resident permit (TRP)

## holder. Only foreign nationals physically in Canada hold temporary resident status.

Foreign nationals such as refugee claimants in Canada and unauthorized workers or those with expired permits, whose work experience would be accumulated while they have no temporary resident status in Canada, are not eligible for the CEC program. Remarks should indicate that the issuance of a permit does not indicate temporary resident status.

### Working with a Visitor Record

An applicant under the CEC does not need to hold a work permit; they only need to have valid TR status during the qualifying work period(s). In other words, applicants who are authorized to work in Canada under R186 and DO NOT hold a work permit, may still be able to apply under the CEC, but must provide

## documentation with their application establishing that they had legal temporary status in Canada (e.g., a

visitor record for religious workers). A visitor record is a status document issued to both visa-required or visa-exempt foreign nationals. A visitor record may be issued at a POE, to a foreign national seeking to enter Canada, or to one who is already in Canada and wishes to either:

- extend their stay in Canada beyond their initial authorized stay;
- restore their status as a temporary resident in Canada, following a loss of their status; or
- change the conditions of their stay
A visitor record issued to someone who intends to perform authorized work, verifies the status of the temporary resident as work permit exempt and supports their application to Service Canada for their social insurance number. A visitor record issued in this case should include remarks specifying the ability of the

### Working with a Temporary Resident Permit

In some cases an officer may issue a TRP to allow a person who is inadmissible, or who does not meet the requirements of the IRPA, to become a temporary resident (that is, to enter or remain in Canada) if it is justified in the circumstances. A temporary resident permit (TRP) confers temporary resident status and as such, applicants who obtained their qualifying work experience while in Canada on a TRP are eligible to apply for the CEC. These applicants are eligible as long as their work in Canada was authorized. Keep in mind that applicants who are inadmissible to Canada cannot be granted permanent residence as members of the CEC. However, this does not preclude the foreign national from applying for permanent residence under the CEC

# program, nor including work performed while in Canada under a TRP.

The key factor for a reviewing officer to consider is whether the PA held valid temporary resident status during their qualifying work period, as they must meet R186 requirements to be authorized to work pursuant to

## R87.1(3)(b), and must hold temporary resident status throughout the qualifying period.

### Maintained or “Implied” Status

A foreign national may work in Canada without a work permit until a decision is made on an application to renew/extend a work permit, if:

- they have applied before expiry of original work permit and
- they remained in Canada after the expiry of their work permit and
- they have continued to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, other than the expiry date; (work for employer on WP, NOC, and location, if applicable)

If a visitor, student or temporary worker applies to extend their status, prior to the expiry of that status, they may legally remain in Canada until a decision is made on the application. In this situation, the person is considered to have maintained legal status as a temporary resident. Section R201 allows foreign nationals to apply for a renewal of their work permit from within Canada, only if the application is made before their

## present work permit expires. Paragraph R186(u) authorizes foreign nationals to work without a permit

(“implied status") when they have submitted an application under section R201 and a decision on the renewal application has not yet been made.

## Work experience acquired during a period of maintained status will be considered as eligible work

experience under the CEC, provided the applicant continued to work in Canada under the same conditions as their original work permit until a decision was made on their application for a work permit extension.

Note: “Implied" or maintained status only applies up until a decision is made on the original work permit

renewal application. The implied status expires on the date that a decision is made on the application to

## extend or renew the original permit. The application may be approved, refused or withdrawn.

Once the original work permit expires, the foreign national cannot submit another application under section R201, because they no longer have a valid work permit. In the 90 days following the expiry of the permit, the foreign national is considered to be without status, by may be able to apply to restore their TR Page | 38

This means that if the foreign national in Canada does not apply to renew their permit prior to its expiry, while they may be eligible for restoration of status, they may not apply to extend or renew the permit AND they are no longer authorized to work. ## Restoration of Status

If a temporary resident in Canada does not apply to extend or renew their work permit, study permit or visitor record prior to expiry, then they are considered to have lost their TR status on the date their permit expired. If a visitor, worker or student has lost their status, they may apply to reinstate or restore their status in accordance with section 182 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations. Contrary to applicants with implied status, persons awaiting restoration have lost their status and may not continue to work.

Language

In order to meet the MEC for the CEC program, according to R87.1(d) and (e) of the IRPR, at the time of application, an applicant must identify which of English or French is to be considered their first official language and which is to be considered their second official language, and must be assessed by a designated organization and submit the results of that assessment with their application. The applicant must evaluated against the Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB) for English and the Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadien (NCLC) for French, and must achieve minimum scores for reading, writing, speaking and listening. For the CEC program, the applicant must meet minimum language thresholds as follows:

- Canadian Language Benchmark 7 for TEER 0 and TEER 1 jobs Canadian Language Benchmark 5 for TEER 2 and TEER 3 jobs
If an applicant has work experience in both TEER 0 and TEER 1 as well as TEER 2 and TEER 3 occupations, the applicant must satisfy the officer that they meet the minimum language proficiency threshold for the skill type/level in which they have obtained most (i.e., more than half) of their qualifying work experience [R87.1(2)(e)].

Note: If an applicant has work experience that is split evenly between TEER 0,1 or TEER 2, 3 occupations, the

officer should apply the language proficiency threshold that is most favorable to the applicant.

The following test results are acceptable evidence of language proficiency:

IELTS (International English Language Testing System) administered by the British Council, the University of Cambridge and Education Australia; CELPIP (Canadian English Language Proficiency Index Program), administered by the University of British Columbia; TEF (Test d’évaluation du français) administered by Chambre de commerce de Paris (Alliance Française abroad); and TCF Canada: Test de connaissance du français, administered by Centre international d'études pédagogiques (CIEP) for the French Ministry of Education

- PTE Core: Pearson Test of English, you must take the PTE CORE option
Applicants are only required to submit their test reference number. Language test results are verified by CiO Program Assistants at the time of completeness check. Points are awarded based on equivalency grids.

Language test results must be valid (less than two years old) both when the applicant

- completes the Express Entry profile; AND
- applies for permanent residence

Education

There is no education requirement included in the Minimum Entry Criteria for the CEC program. Applicants may be awarded points on the CRS grid for education credentials, and therefore an assessment of education credentials may be required. Applicants must submit either their completed Canadian educational credential or their completed foreign educational credential along with an equivalency assessment (Educational Credential Assessment [ECA] report) issued by a designated assessment organization or institution with their application for permanent residence. The equivalency assessment must be less than five years old on the date on which their application is made [EE MI's s.11(5); R75(2)(e)].

Education Credential Assessments (ECA)

Equivalency assessments (ECA reports) will be used as conclusive evidence that the applicant's completed foreign diplomas, certificates or credentials are equivalent to completed Canadian educational credentials. The ECA report will also include an assessment by the organization or institution of the authenticity of the completed foreign diploma, certificate or credential.

If a professional body has been designated for the primary occupation specified in the application, the applicant must submit a completed foreign diploma, certificate or credential relevant to that occupation and the equivalency assessment (ECA report) issued by the designated professional body establishing that the completed foreign diploma, certificate or credential is equivalent to the completed Canadian educational credential required to practice that occupation in at least one of the provinces in which the equivalency assessments issued by this professional body are recognized.

Only reports issued by an IRCC-designated organization or institution will be accepted as an equivalency assessment for the purpose of a federal skilled worker class application.

Applicants are only required to submit their ECA reference number, not a copy of their assessment. ECA reports are also verified by CiO Program Assistants at the time of the completeness check. Applicants must declare in their Express Entry profile if they have obtained an ECA for their foreign educational credential. An ECA report must be less than five years old at the time the Express Entry profile is submitted and upon receipt of the application for permanent residence. CRS points are awarded for the highest level of education obtained [EE MI's s. 11(2). Maximum CRS points awarded for education are 150 without a spouse and 140 with a spouse. Points may also be awarded for a spouse's education provided above requirements are met, up to a maximum of 10 points.

ECA reports are only accepted if the report was issued _after_the organization was designated as an ECA provided for IRCC. There are 7 designated ECA providers as follows: World Education Services (WES): Date of Designation: April 17, 2013 Comparative Education Service: University of Toronto School of Continuing Studies: Date of Designation: April 17, 2013 International Credential Assessment Service of Canada: Date of Designation: April 17, 2013 Medical Council of Canada: Date of Designation: April 17, 2013 Pharmacy Examining Board of Canada (PEBC): Date of Designation: January 6, 2014 International Credential Evaluation Service (ICES): Date of Designation: August 6, 2015

- International Qualifications Assessment Service (IQAS): Date of Designation: August 6, 2015

## CRS: Job Offer

A qualifying job offer / offer of arranged employment is defined in subsection 29(2) of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system, and in R82 of the IRPR.

A job offer is considered to be a “qualifying offer of arranged employment" if it is for continuous, paid, full-time work that is, not seasonal, in TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 of the National Occupational Classification (NOC) matrix, is for at least one year after issuance of visa for permanent residence, and if it meets one of the following three conditions:

1. the employer making the job offer has a positive Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) from Employment and Social Development Canada that approves the offer and names the candidate and their position; or
2. the candidate •is currently working in Canada in a TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 job on a work permit that was issued based
on an LMIA, is working for an employer listed on the work permit, is authorized to work in Canada when submitting their application and when the visa is issued, and has received a job offer from their employer for a full-time job in TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 for at least one year after becoming a permanent resident; or

3. the candidate has a valid work permit for a job in TEER 0, 1, 2, or 3 that is exempt from needing an LMIA (under an international agreement such as the North America Free Trade Agreement, a federal- provincial agreement, or other cases supporting Canadian interests) and the candidate (LMIA is exempt work permit under R204 (a) or (c) or R205):
- is currently working for an employer specified on the work permit has accumulated one year of full-time work experience (or an equal amount of part-time work) and has a valid job offer from that employer for at least one year after their visa for permanent residence is issued.
REMEMBER: The employer must be named on the LMIA-exempt work permit. An ‘open' work permit would not meet this requirement.

## 4) Go to Employment tab; click [W/E Multipull] on ADMM.

## Updating the decision in GCMS

In addition to the 11.2-EE MI decision, since March 2020 agents are now also updating the Selection-EE Econ decision. In the same view as above, once you have entered a decision for A11.2 you will hit New and in the "Type" field choose Selection-EE Econ from the drop-down list. Decisions should be updated according to the following scenarios.

11.2-EE MI = Met Selection-EE Econ = Passed No concerns with A11.2 CRS allocations as per the Ministerial Instructions Reserved for situations where the client has provided objective evidence of work experience, including skill level, duties and period of employment. Client has provided evidence of their education and language skills, as applicable. Client has provided sufficient settlement funds, when required.
Note: This status can be used in cases where large deposits may be identified. If the client meets the
 minimum amount for settlement funds, do not reference the large deposit in your A11.2 note as this large deposit should be reviewed by a Case Processing Officer. See below for further instructions.
11.2-EE MI = Met Selection-EE Econ = Recommend Passed
