# Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

Canadian immigration and refugee law concerns the area of law related to the admission of foreign nationals* into Canada, their rights and responsibilities once admitted, and the conditions of their removal. The primary law on these matters is the "Immigration and Refugee Protection Act"(IRPA).

“foreign national" means a person who is not a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident and includes a stateless person. A foreign national may be outside Canada or already in Canada.

“permanent resident" of Canada refers to a person who has acquired resident status under IRPA, and not subsequently lost that status.

The "Immigration and Refugee Protection Act"(IRPA) is an Act of the Parliament of Canada, passed in 2002, and is the primary federal legislation regulating immigration to Canada. It replaced the "Immigration Act" of 1976.

How to read IRPA The legislation is composed of two main parts: The Act and The Regulations. Throughout this manual, references to “the Act" include regulations made under it as well.

IRPA creates a high level framework detailing the goals and guidelines the Canadian government has set with regard to immigration into Canada by foreign residents. The Regulations contain the laws created to fit within the IRPA in order to specify how the IRPA is to be applied.

Sections of IRPA are commonly preceded by an “A" (ie. A12), whereas sections of the Regulations are

## commonly preceded by an “R” (ie. R70).

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canadaet Citoyenneté Canada L'information divulguée en vertu de la [oi sur l'accès à Finformatior Objectives and Application

Some main objectives of this Act with respect to immigration are:

- to permit Canada to pursue the maximum social, cultural and economic benefits of immigration;
- to see that families are reunited in Canada;
- to protect public health and safety and to maintain the security of Canadian society;
- to promote international justice and security by fostering respect for human rights and by denying access to Canadian territory to persons who are criminals or security risks; and
- to offer safe haven to persons with a well-founded fear of persecution based on race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group, as well as those at risk of torture or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment;

This Act is to be applied in a manner that:

(a) furthers the domestic and international interests of Canada;

(b) promotes accountability and transparency by enhancing public awareness of immigration and refugee programs;

(c) facilitates cooperation between the Government of Canada, provincial governments, foreign states, international organizations and non-governmental organizations;

(d) ensures that decisions taken under this Act are consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, including its principles of equality and freedom from discrimination and of the equality of English and French as the official languages of Canada;

(e) supports the commitment of the Government of Canada to enhance the vitality of the English and French linguistic minority communities in Canada; and

(f) complies with international human rights instruments to which Canada is signatory

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canadaet Citoyenneté Canada Information disclosed under the Access to Information Act L'nformation divulguée en vertu de la toi sur l’accès à Tinformation Permanent Residents IRPA provides the rules by which a foreign national can be deemed inadmissible or denied entry to Canada; be admitted to Canada on a temporary basis; obtain status in Canada as a Permanent Resident; maintain their status in Canada; and more. The following section highlights some important sections of the act and regulations.

Requirements Before Entering Canada

A11. (1) A foreign national must, before entering Canada, apply to an officer for a visa or for any other document required by the regulations. The visa or document may be issued if, following an examination, the officer is satisfied that the foreign national is not inadmissible and meets the requirements of this Act.

A16. (1) A person who makes an application must answer truthfully all questions put to them for the purpose of the examination and must produce a visa and all relevant evidence and documents that the officer reasonably requires.

A18. (1) Every person seeking to enter Canada must appear for an examination to determine whether that person has a right to enter Canada or is or may become authorized to enter and remain in Canada.

Upon Entry

A20. (1) Every foreign national who seeks to enter or remain in Canada must establish,

(a) to become a permanent resident, that they hold the visa or other document required under the regulations and have come to Canada in order to establish permanent residence; and
(b) to become a temporary resident, that they hold the visa or other document required under the regulations and will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay
A21. (1) A foreign national becomes a permanent resident if an officer is satisfied that the foreign national has applied for that status, has met the obligations set out in paragraph 20(1)(a) and subsection 20(2) and is not inadmissible.

Dual intent

(2) An intention by a foreign national to become a permanent resident does not preclude them from becoming a temporary resident if the officer is satisfied that they will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay. Economic Class A12(2) A foreign national may be selected as a member of the economic class on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada.

One of the three Classes of immigration and permanent residence is the Economic Class, which includes applicants who will be assessed on the skills and/or expertise they could bring to Canada. The economic

## permanent resident applicants are assessed against a selection system based on a category. These categories

are:

Federal skilled worker

## Provincial nominee

Canadian Experience

- Federal Skilled Trades
### Federal Skilled Worker (FSW)

This program is designed for applicants who are skilled workers, who may become permanent residents on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada, and who intend to reside in a province other than Quebec. Successful applicants must have a minimum of one year of “skilled" work experience and meet the minimum requirements for education, language abilities as well as other requirements to demonstrate their ability to successfully establish themselves in Canada.

### Provincial nominee (PNP)

Another type of independent permanent resident applicant is a provincial nominee. Applicants under this category are selected in consultation with the province interested in making the nomination. In some cases

## provinces will seek to nominate applicants with experience in occupations considered “in demand" within that

province. Applicants holding a provincial nomination must also meet federal requirements for admissibility.

### Canadian Experience (CEC)

The Canadian Experience Class is prescribed as a class of persons who may become permanent residents on the basis of their Canadian experience and who:

- intend to reside in a province or territory other than Quebec;
- have acquired a minimum of one year work experience in Canada;
- have maintained temporary resident status during their qualifying period of work experience in Canada; and
- meet the language requirement.
## Federal Skilled Trades (FST)

The Federal Skilled Trades Program is for people who want to become permanent residents based on being qualified in a skilled trade.

To apply, you must have work experience in a specific skilled trade and meet several other requirements.

Intent to reside

Applicants will indicate within their Express Entry application where they intend to reside when they become a permanent resident. Applicants who indicate an intention to reside in the province of Quebec are not eligible to apply under the FSW program. If you have concerns about the applicant's intention to reside in a province other than Quebec, the file should be referred to an officer for review. Keep in mind that an applicant's experience (either prior or current) in a province does not necessarily denote an intention to live there in the future.

## The Process

Economic Class applications for permanent residence are submitted to the Centralized Intake Office at CPC-Sydney in Nova Scotia. The ClO checks the application for completeness, creates the application in the electronic database, and process the payment. In some cases CiO completes the assessment and finalizes the application for permanent residence. More complex cases are forwarded to other offices in the Domestic, International or Centralized Network for continued processing. Triage criteria have been developed to determine which applications are referred to other offices, and at which stage of processing the referral will take place.

After meeting specific eligibility criteria for the particular program as described above, all applicants still need to be admissible in order to be granted the status of Permanent Resident. Generally this would include a medical screening and background checks for criminality and security. Once all members of the family meet all requirements, each individual is issued a permanent resident visa that is processed when they arrive in Canada.

There are several Economic Class programs which are eligible for processing under EE, including: Federal Skilled Workers, Canadian Experience Class, Federal Skilled Trades, and certain Provincial Nominees.

Section 11.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) includes a new authority that supports the Express Entry system, and adds a new level of decision making for permanent residence applications. Under A11.2, we are able to refuse an EE application when the applicant does not meet minimum entry criteria (MEC) or did not or does not possess the qualifications for which they received their invitation to apply.

The 11.2 decisions for Federal Skilled Worker applications will be the focus of this training. In the next module you will be introduced to some key concepts related to the Express Entry application management system, and look at both the requirement to maintain the MEC, and the requirement to prove and maintain the self- declared qualifications for which they were awarded points resulting in the invitation to apply.

# Introduction to Express Entry

Express Entry is an application management system. It is a method of ranking potential immigration candidates,

## choosing those with the highest qualifications and inviting them to apply for permanent residence. Candidates,

or potential applicants, get the benefit of more efficient processing and accelerated processing times. For IRCC, it is a way for our department to better manage the intake of economic class applications and prevent backlogs (at least at the intake stage), while providing consistent, efficient processing for applicants.

Candidates create an online Express Entry profile in their MyCIC account and, if invited to apply, submit their application for permanent residence (APR) through their MyCIC account.

Express Entry POOL

Application Express Entry1 – MINIMUM ENTRY CRITERIA 2 – COMPREHENSIVE 3 – INVITATION TO APPLY for permanent Submission AND POINTS SCORE RANKING SYSTEM residence

### Business Process

Foreign nationals who are interested in living in Canada permanently and who have work experience in a skilled occupation, may register and create a personal secure online account in with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada. During this process, potential applicants (Candidates) will enter information related to their:

Age Level of education Language abilities Work experience

- Family members Details related to any job offers in Canada
The system will determine whether the foreign national meets the Minimum Entry Criteria (MEC) for any of the eligible programs for Express Entry processing, and assign a value to each applicable aspect according to the MEC.

When a candidate's profile shows that they meet the minimum entry criteria (MEC), the system automatically enters their profile into the Express Entry pool. Potential candidates MUST meet the criteria for one of the

## programs set up for EE in order to get into the pool.

Candidates receive a notification letting them know when their profile has been placed in the EE pool, and that their profile will remain in the pool for 365 days. This notification gives the candidate their score and ranking as well as detailed instructions for next steps, including instruction to begin gathering documents to support the claims they have made when creating their profile. While in the pool, the candidate may update their profile at any time. Page | 12

Candidates need their Job Seeker validation code to register for the Government of Canada's Job Bank, an electronic listing of jobs provided by employers from across Canada. Candidates without a job offer or a provincial or territorial nomination will be required to register with the Job Bank to complete and submit their Express Entry profile. Express Entry candidates can be matched with Canadian employers and jobs based on their skills, knowledge and experience.

At this point, the candidate is eligible to receive an Invitation to Apply (ITA) for the program whose requirements they appear to meet. A specific number of invitations are issued (ITA) on a regular, usually bi-weekly basis, to Express Entry candidates who have the highest Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) scores at the time of an Express Entry round of invitations. Those who receive an ITA have 60 days to apply. This deadline is indicated in the client's correspondence, which they can access in their MyCiC account. Candidates who are issued an ITA have three options: they can respond to the ITA; they can ignore it (in which case they are removed from the Express Entry pool); they can decline it, in which case they return to the pool for consideration in future rounds of invitations. Candidates may ONLY apply for permanent residence online if they receive an invitation to apply through the Express Entry system. Completing an online Express Entry profile or entering the pool doesn't guarantee that a candidate will be invited to apply for permanent residence.

A foreign national is considered to be a “CANDIDATE" up until he/she submits an application for permanent residence (APR). Once an application is submitted he/she is considered to be an “APPLICANT”.

Comprehensive Ranking System The Comprehensive Ranking System, or CRS, is a points-based system used to assess and score a candidate's

Express Entry profile and determine a candidate's position in the Express Entry pool. It ranks prospective skilled immigrants by looking at their skills, work experience, language ability, education and other factors that we know lead to success in Canada. Each candidate in the Express Entry pool is ranked according to points awarded for certain economic selection factors. A candidate's total score is known as the CRS score.

According to A10.3(1) and A87.3(3), the minister may give instructions with respect to the way immigration applications are processed. From time to time such Ministerial Instructions are released to guide our processing, and these instructions should be applied in conjunction with IRPA.

The Express Entry application management system is primarily governed using Ministerial Instructions. Throughout the training we will refer to the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system. We use these Ministerial Instructions to guide us in our decision making, specifically the decisions we make related

# to A11.2. Further decisions related to program eligibility and inadmissibility require the application of program

regulations and other specific sections of IRPA.

As required by IRPA, subsection 10.3(4), all Ministerial Instructions related to Express Entry must be published on IRCC's website. Some Ministerial Instructions must also be posted in the Canada Gazette. The Ministerial

# Instructions respecting the Express Entry system came into force on January 1, 2015

### CRS points and the Ministerial Instructions

According to Section 8 of the Current Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system, the total number of points that may be assigned under the Comprehensive Ranking System is 1200 points, allocated as follows:

- (a) for the core human capital factors o (i) a maximum of 500 points if the foreign national has no accompanying spouse or common-law
partner, or o(ii) a maximum of 460 points if the foreign national has an accompanying spouse or common-law partner;

(b) for accompanying spouse or common-law partner factors, a maximum of 40 points;
(c) for skill transferability factors, a maximum of 100 points; and
(d) for additional factors, a maximum of 600 points.

Intake: Receiving an Application for Permanent Residence submitted via Express Entry Applicants are required to submit a complete electronic application for permanent residence (e-APR) within 60 calendar days of being issued an invitation to apply (ITA). The application and all supporting documents must be submitted electronically through the applicant's online account.

Applications are assessed for completeness up front at the CiO. An application found to be incomplete is rejected as per Section 10 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, and all fees associated with the application should be refunded to the applicant.

The Express Entry six-month processing standard begins when an application is assessed as complete and is promoted in the Global Case Management System (GCMS). It ends when Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) makes a final decision on the application.

A complete application must include the cost recovery fees and all supporting documentation to validate information contained in the applicant's Express Entry profile and e-APR.

Applicants and their family members must undergo upfront medical examinations and submit all required police certificates as part of their complete application. Medical results must be valid and applicants are encouraged to undergo medical examinations closer to the date their application is submitted to avoid processing delays.

A personalized document checklist is produced for each applicant when they submit their e-APR through their online account. The personalized checklist identifies the specific supporting documents required from each family member included on the application.

The following documents are mandatory and must be provided by all applicants.

Applications that do not contain the following documents are rejected as incomplete, and fees are refunded accordingly.

- Medical examination confirmation-for all family members, whether accompanying or not (Temporary Public Policy currently in effect, review current process) ●Police certificates – for the principal applicant and all family members 18 years of age or older, whether accompanying or not Copy of the biographical data page of a passport or travel document – required for all
- Proof of work experience – for the PA only

# A11.2 Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

Visa or other document not to be issued

11.2 (1) An officer may not issue a visa or other document in respect of an application for permanent residence to a foreign national who was issued an invitation to make that application if — at the time the invitation was issued or at the time the officer received their application — the foreign national did not meet the criteria set out in an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(e) or did not have the qualifications on the basis of which they were ranked under an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(h) and were issued the invitation. Exceptions
(2) Despite subsection (1), an officer may issue the visa or other document if, at the time the officer received their application,
(a) the foreign national did not meet the criteria set out in an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(e) — or did not have the qualifications on the basis of which they were ranked under an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(h) — because the applicant's birthday occurred after the invitation was issued; or
(b) the foreign national did not have the qualifications they had at the time the invitation was issued and on the basis of which they were ranked under an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(h), but
### (i) they met the criteria set out in an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1)(e), and

(ii) they occupied a rank that is not lower than the rank that a foreign national was required to have occupied to be invited to make an application.

According to A11.2 when reviewing an application, processing offices must determine if

- the applicant possesses the qualifications that they declared in their e-APR, as corroborated by the applicant's supporting documentation; and •when the applicant submits their e-APR, the information provided in their Express Entry profile has not materially changed to the degree that the applicant would not have been issued an ITA in that round of invitations.
Processing offices must compare the information in the applicant's profile at the time of the round of invitations to the information in their e-APR to ensure that the applicant meets the requirements of section A11.2. Note that not all discrepancies should result in a refusal (A11.2(2)).

#### Requirement to maintain the MEC

A11.2 specifies that applicants must meet the criteria set out in A10.3(e) to be accepted into the Express Entry pool and must also meet this criteria when they are issued an ITA and when they submit their e-APR.

10.3 (1) The Minister may give instructions governing any matter relating to the application of this Division, including instructions respecting (e)the criteria that a foreign national must meet to be eligible to be invited to make an application;

The criteria referred to in this subsection is otherwise known as the “Minimum Entry Criteria” for the program in which the applicant is applying. Ministerial Instructions for Express Entry list the Minimum Entry Criteria (MEC) for each program. If you determine that the applicant did not meet the MEC for the program at the time he/she was invited to apply, the application should be refused. If an applicant's situation changes in the time between when they receive an ITA and when they submit their e-APR to such a degree that they no longer meet the MEC, the application must be refused under section A11.2. An officer will need to consider whether the application should be refused for not meeting the minimum requirements of the federal program to which they are applying, or for misrepresentation (A40).

## Requirement to maintain the CRS score

A11.2 also specifies that an applicant must have the qualifications described in 10.3(1)(h) of IRPA at the time they are issued the invitation to apply and at the time the application is received.

10.3 (1) The Minister may give instructions governing any matter relating to the application of this Division, including instructions respecting (h) the basis on which an eligible foreign national may be ranked relative to other eligible foreign nationals

The name of the system or basis on which EE candidates are ranked is the “Comprehensive Ranking System”. Candidates are awarded a score for each of their self-declared qualifications. These scores are totaled and amount to the candidate's CRS score. When a round of invitations occurs, IRCC invites the top-ranked candidates in the Express Entry pool to apply for permanent residence. After each round of invitations, IRCC publishes the score of the lowest-ranked candidate to receive an ITA in that round of invitations.

An applicant's CRS score is automatically recorded in GCMS at the time when
- their ITA is issued; and
- their e-APR is submitted.

Applicants are required to maintain the qualifications that led them to be included in the top-ranked candidates to be issued an ITA in a particular round of invitations. At the time of the e-APR, processing officers should compare both CRS scores to determine which of the following scenarios should be applied:

• If the applicant's CRS score at the time of the e-APR is equal to or higher than the lowest-ranked score in the round of invitations, the application will not be refused under section A11.2, as long as the applicant's supporting documentation corroborates their claims and they continue to meet the MEC for Express Entry, including the requirements of the program to which they were invited to apply. If the applicant's CRS score at the time of the e-APR is lower than the lowest-ranked score in the round of invitations, the application should be refused under section A11.2 for not having maintained the qualifications that would justify the ITA. The main exception to this is those applicants who lost points because they had a birthday between ITA and the submission of their e-APR – see the example scenario below.

Ministerial Instructions related to the CRS are revised periodically. Applications must be assessed under section A11.2 according to the Ministerial Instructions in force during the round of invitations to which the

In other words, an applicant's CRS score at the time of the ITA and at the time of application should be calculated based on the Ministerial Instructions in place at the time of the ITA.

Exemption to section A11.2(1): candidates whose birthday occurs after they receive an ITA

An applicant may have a birthday after they receive an ITA but before they submit their e-APR. Their change in age may lower their CRS score below the lowest score in the round of invitations. It may also result in the applicant no longer meeting the minimum requirements of the FSWC and, consequently, no longer meeting the MEC, resulting in a refusal based on section A11.2

When a change in age results in the candidate no longer meeting the MEC or having their recalculated CRS points score fall below the lowest points score in that round of invitations, processing offices will apply the exemption in A11.2(2).

Example scenario: candidate has a birthday between ITA and e-APR

Jan is 35 years old when she receives her ITA. She has met the MEC and has 67 points on the FSWC points grid. Between her ITA and e-APR, Jan turns 36. She now has 66 points on the FSWC points grid, no longer meets the program requirements of FSWC and, consequently, no longer meets the MEC. Due to her change in age, Jan's CRS score drops by 5 points, putting her below the lowest-ranked candidate in her round of invitations.

The officer grants Jan the exemption and, consequently, Jan continues to meet the MEC. This also exempts Jan from being refused under section A11.2 for her adjusted CRS score and for not meeting program requirements.

### Examining the FSW Minimum Entry Criteria

IRPA defines the classes in which foreign nationals can apply to immigrate to Canada, and requirements for each class and category/program within a class (program eligibility); selection factors that influence the individual's ability to become economically established (Selection); and grounds for inadmissibility to Canada

All programs included in Express Entry fall under the Economic Class. The Economic Class is generally prescribed as a class of persons who are skilled workers, who may become permanent residents on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada.

The Federal Skilled Worker category is FSW category is for applicants who intend to reside in a province other than Quebec, and who have work experience in an occupation at TEER 0, 1, 2 or 3 skill level. The Minimum Entry Criteria (MEC) required for a Federal Skilled Worker are:

- Skilled work experience Language ability
- Education

In addition, applicants must also meet the following FSW selection factors to meet the Minimum Entry Criteria: ●Sufficient funds required for settlement (or an approved job offer); and

- Minimum 67 points from a combination of the six FSW selection factors
### Regulatory Reference:

A10.3(1)(e) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations and Section 5 of the Ministerial Instructions for Express Entry state that in order to be eligible for Express Entry processing, an applicant must be a “member of the class", or meet the minimum requirements of one of the three following federal economic programs: the Federal Skilled Worker class; the Canadian Experience Class; or the Federal Skilled Trades class. The Ministerial Instructions defer to the regulations for the definition of who is a member of a class for each program.

R75 and R76 define the minimum requirements for a Federal Skilled Worker, and so we apply these regulations in order to determine whether the MEC has been met.

R75(2) A foreign national is a skilled worker if

(a) within the last 10 years they have accumulated, over a continuous period, at least one year of full- time work experience, or the equivalent in part-time work, in the occupation identified by the foreign national in their application as their primary occupation that is listed in Skill Type 0 Management Occupations or Skill Level A or B of the National Occupational Classification matrix;

(b) performed the actions described in the lead statement for the occupation;

(c) performed a substantial number of the main duties of the occupation;

Introduction to the NOC and NOC Matrix

NOC The National Occupational Classification (NOC) is the nationally accepted reference on occupations in Canada. It is used analyze and communicate information about occupations, and to understand the jobs found throughout Canada's labour market. The NOC is a standard that classifies and describes the occupations in the Canadian economy.

#### NOC Matrix

The NOC Matrix provides an overview of the entire occupational classification structure for jobs in Canada, based on Skill Levels and Broad Occupational Categories or Types of occupations. Skill Levels are represented in the columns while the Skill Types are found in rows. Senior Management and other Managerial occupations are found in the first column of the chart, indicating the presence of management across all segments of the labour market.

5 Occupations in art, culture, recreation and sport 6 Sales and service occupations 7 Trades, transport and equipment operators and related occupations 8 Natural resources, agriculture and related production occupations 9 Occupations in manufacturing and utilities

## Reviewing the NOC website:

Each NOC description includes the following elements:

Lead Statement The lead statement provides a general description of the occupation and the boundaries of the unit group. It also indicates the kinds of industries, workplaces or establishments where the occupation is found. Applicants must have performed the actions in the lead statement in order to include the period of work experience in the stated NOC.

Example Titles Example titles are the occupational titles commonly found within the group. This list is an extraction of a more expansive listing of alphabetical job titles found in the NOC Index of Titles. The example titles may help to determine if the work experience is in the stated NOC.

Page | 30

A-2025-58066-000425

Immigration, Refugees mmigration, Réfugiés and Citizenship Canadaet Citoyenneté Canada L'nformation divulguée en vertu de la toi sur l’accès à Tinformation Main Duties The main duties section describes the most significant duties of the occupations in the group. Depending on the Unit Group, it may include:

- a series of statements that can be applied to all occupations in the group;
- two or more sub-sets of occupations with statements that apply to each sub-set or component; and/or
- a series of brief statements that are linked to specific occupations, that, while similar enough to be in the same group, can be described separately.

Statements in Italics, at the end of this section, identify a specialization that may exist within the occupation. Employment requirements are prerequisites generally needed to enter the occupation. Several types of requirements are listed: type and level of education including specific subject matter if relevant, starting with the lowest possible requirement for entry into the occupation; specific training required, including apprenticeship, on-the-job or internal training; experience in a related occupation, especially for supervisory or managerial occupations; licenses, certificates or affiliations; and/or

- other requirements not dependent on formal education, such as athletic abilities, artistic talent or presentation of a portfolio.

While some occupations have very specific employment requirements, others have a wide range of acceptable requirements. The following terminology is used to indicate the level of the requirement: "Is required" indicates a definite requirement. "Is usually required" means that the qualification is generally expressed as required by a majority of employers, but not always mandatory. "May be required" describes requirements that some employers may impose, but are not universal.

*Note – for FSW, it is not necessary that the employment requirements be met; the regulations specify must have performed lead statement and main duties.

Additional Information

Some descriptions include additional information to give details on: Mobility patterns; • Progression to supervisory positions, specializations or to other occupations such as management;

- Other information that may clarify the occupational description

This information can sometimes be helpful when determining whether work experience performed actually meets the requirements of the stated NOC, particularly when the duties listed in the work experience documentation are not a “substantial" number. Experience should be assessed “on balance of probabilities" to determine whether it is more likely that they have the stated work experience, than not. To determine whether the applicant has the requisite work experience, the main duties listed in the letters from the employer are assessed and compared against the information in the National Occupational Classification (Noc) website. #### Canadian Work Experience

## "Status” and “authorization" are separate in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). Canadian

work must be authorized, and it must be performed while the applicant has valid TR status. A foreign national may have TR status and not be authorized to work.

#### Definition of “work” [R2]

“Work" is defined in the Regulations as an activity for which wages are paid or commission is earned, or that competes directly with activities of Canadian citizens or permanent residents in the Canadian labour market

# [R2].

Authorized Work

Work may be authorized for foreign nationals in Canada either with a work permit, or through another regulatory authority. Work permits may be issued to either visa-required or visa-exempt foreign nationals. Work permits may be employer-driven, based on a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA), or they may be LMIA-exempt. Some temporary residents may be authorized to work without a work permit in certain situations. Keep in mind that work experience gained through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits while a full-time student and on-campus work permits, does not meet the requirements for CRS points. Whether work is performed with or without a work permit, you must ensure both that the work period was

### authorized AND that the foreign national held temporary resident status at the time.

#### Work Permits

### Conditions

Work permits are always issued with conditions. For example, all temporary residents have an automatically imposed condition that they must leave Canada at the end of their authorized period of stay. Specific conditions related to temporary work are imposed by an officer and are specific to the client's situation. It is important you understand the imposed conditions such as:

- a period of authorized stay the type of work the employer location of work times and period of work
### Period of authorized stay

A work permit will always indicate the period authorized for stay in Canada (ie. Expiry date). The authorized period of stay may be longer than the authorized period of work [R185(a) and R185(b)(iv)].

Type of work There are a variety of situations where the type of work/occupation is restricted. There are employer-specific

## work permits and also “open” employer work permits that are occupation-restricted [R185(b)(i)]. Employer-

specific work permits are issued for foreign nationals to work in a specific occupation, for a specific employer. These work permits are employer-driven, where the employer must apply for and receive an LMiA* before the foreign national can apply for a work permit, or must issue an offer of employment for LMIA-exempt workers [R204-R208]. “Open" restricted work permit: Where the employer is not listed, a location and/or occupation may be restricted. An occupation may be restricted due to medical or program requirements. For example, the person may not be able to work in jobs where the protection of the public health is required, if they have been assessed as M2, M3, or M4.

*LMIA: Labour Market Impact Assessment, or an assessment — provided to the officer by the Department of Employment and Social Development that the requirements set out in subsection 203(1) with respect to the offer have been met

#### The employer

### Work permits issued under R200(1)(c)(ii.1) will identify the employer. The employer name will match the

employer named on the LMIA or the offer of employment. When an officer issues an employer-specific work permit under an LMIA exemption, GCMS will automatically insert the employer's name into the “Employer" field.

#### Location of work

Location of work must be imposed as a condition where an LMIA has been issued or where it is a requirement of the LMIA exemption [R185(b)(iii)]. For example, when an employer has several franchise locations but indicates only one location on the offer of employment, the work permit should reflect the physical location of work and restrict the work to that location. However, if the employer indicates in the offer of employment that the worker will be working at multiple work locations, the officer should not restrict the work permit to a single location and should indicate in the "Remarks" field that the worker is authorized to work at the various locations across Canada. For LMIA- supported work permits, the location of work must match the destination on the LMIA. For LMIA-exempt work permits, if the location of work is important to the exemption (such as for provincial nominees), then the location will be specified and the restriction on location imposed.

#### Times and periods of work

While the period of authorized stay may extend beyond the authorization period of work, the period of work may never extend beyond the duration specified in the LMIA or offer of employment. There may also be conditions where worker is not authorized to work at specific times or dates. For example, seasonal agricultural workers are never to work between December 15 and January 1; students are automatically authorized to work

## for up to 20 hours per week in their off-campus employment during the semester.

Post-graduation work permit (PGWP): LMIA-exemption code C43

They are considered “open” work permits, and are coded in GCMS as C43. With a post-graduation work permit, as with all open work permits, graduates can work full time, work part time, or be self-employed. A post-graduation work permit may be issued based on the length of the study program for a minimum of 8 months up to a maximum of 3 years. When determining the length of a post-graduation work permit, officers may consider the duration of the program of study in Canada. When assessing work performed while under a PGWP, officers should assess carefully to ensure that the NOC requirements are met, and that the applicant was not self-employed.

Bridging Work permit (BOWP): LMIA-exemption code A75 Requirements for a bridging open WP are:

- they are currently in Canada;
- they have valid status on a work permit that is due to expire in four months or less;
- they are the principal applicant on an application for permanent residence under FSW, CEC, FST, or PNP they have received a positive eligibility assessment on their permanent residence application under one of the Economic Class programs above (EE: passed A11.2 decision)
- they have applied for an open work permit; and they have paid the work permit processing fee and the Open Work Permit Holder fee For more information: [http://cicintranet.ci.gc.ca/connexion/tools-outils/temp/work-](http://cicintranet.ci.gc.ca/connexion/tools-outils/temp/work-) travail/prov/bridging-transitoires-eng.aspx Validity period for work permits
When determining the validity period of a work permit, officers must first consider the passport validity. A foreign national must hold a passport that is valid for the period authorized for their stay [R52(1)], unless the applicant is exempted (such as U.S. nationals). A work permit cannot be extended beyond the validity of the passport, as doing so would be putting the temporary worker in a position of non-compliance. [Exceptions to this are noted in subsection R52(2)].

As long as the passport is still valid, a work permit will be issued for the complete duration of the LMIA. For LMIA-exempt job offers, the work permit is issued for the expected duration of employment and in some cases longer. Sometimes the duration of the work permit is determined by the maximum time allowed by any particular program or agreement in which the temporary worker is participating.

If a temporary resident visa is necessary, it should have the same duration as the work permit (or passport, if it will expire first), and it should allow for multiple entries where possible. For initial or renewed work permits for visa-exempt foreign nationals: An electronic travel authorization (eTA) will be issued automatically with the work permit. It will be valid for 5 years from the date of issuance or until the client's passport expires (whichever comes first), regardless of whether this date is beyond the expiry date for the work permit.

Working without a Work Permit R186 and R187 describe the types of work which a foreign national is authorized to do without having to obtain a work permit. You can refer to the quick reference guide to occupations to ascertain if applicants are exempt from requiring a work permit. Page | 35

### Temporary resident status

### Admission to Canada

In addition to meeting the eligibility requirements for the temporary resident category under which they have applied, applicants must be authorized to enter Canada – usually this means a foreign national must obtain either a visa or an electronic travel authorization (if they are visa-exempt), which will allow them to enter Canada. A temporary resident visa (TRV) is an official counterfoil document issued by a visa office that is placed in a person's passport to show that they have met the requirements for admission to Canada as a temporary resident. A TRV does not guarantee entry to Canada (ie. Does not give the “right" of entry), nor does it grant temporary resident status in Canada. The border services officer who examines the foreign national upon entry will determine the purpose and duration of the visit. A handwritten date below the stamp indicates the date by which the foreign national must leave Canada. It is at this point that the foreign national receives temporary

# resident status. A temporary resident who leaves Canada will no longer have temporary resident status.

## Status During Period(s) of Work

It is possible for work permits to be issued to those who may not have status as a temporary resident [R202] –

## ie. Refugee claimants who cannot support themselves without working. A foreign national has temporary

resident status when they have been found to meet the requirements of the legislation to enter AND/OR remain in Canada as a visitor, student, worker or temporary resident permit (TRP) holder. Only foreign nationals physically in Canada hold temporary resident status.

### Working with a Visitor Record

An applicant under the FSW does not need to hold a work permit; they only need to have valid TR status during the Canadian work period(s). A visitor record is a status document issued to both visa-required or visa-exempt foreign nationals. A visitor record may be issued at a POE, to a foreign national seeking to enter Canada, or to one who is already in Canada and wishes to either:

- extend their stay in Canada beyond their initial authorized stay;
- restore their status as a temporary resident in Canada, following a loss of their status; or
- change the conditions of their stay

A visitor record issued to someone who intends to perform authorized work, verifies the status of the temporary resident as work permit exempt and supports their application to Service Canada for their social insurance number. A visitor record issued in this case should include remarks specifying the ability of the foreign national to work without a permit. Acceptable remarks that may appear on the visitor record include: "Work permit exempt as a [job title]”; or “Work permit exempt, per section R186”. A foreign national who holds a valid visitor

## record with religious worker”.

### Working with a Temporary Resident Permit

In some cases an officer may issue a TRP to allow a person who is inadmissible, or who does not meet the requirements of the IRPA, to become a temporary resident (that is, to enter or remain in Canada) if it is justified in the circumstances. Page | 36

Maintained or “Implied" Status A foreign national may work in Canada without a work permit until a decision is made on an application to renew/extend a work permit, if:

- they have applied before expiry of original work permit and
- they remained in Canada after the expiry of their work permit and they have continued to comply with the conditions set out on the expired work permit, other than the expiry date; (work for employer on WP, NOC, and location, if applicable)
If a visitor, student or temporary worker applies to extend their status, prior to the expiry of that status, they may legally remain in Canada until a decision is made on the application. In this situation, the person is considered to have maintained legal status as a temporary resident. Section R201 allows foreign nationals to apply for a renewal of their work permit from within Canada, only if the application is made before their present work permit expires. Paragraph R186(u) authorizes foreign nationals to work without a permit (“implied status") when they have submitted an application under section R201 and a decision on the renewal application has not yet been made.

Work experience acquired during a period of maintained status will be considered as eligible work experience, provided the applicant continued to work in Canada under the same conditions as their original work permit until a decision was made on their application for a work permit extension.

Note: “Implied" or maintained status only applies up until a decision is made on the original work permit

renewal application. The implied status expires on the date that a decision is made on the application to extend or renew the original permit. The application may be approved, refused or withdrawn.

Once the original work permit expires, the foreign national cannot submit another application under section R201, because they no longer have a valid work permit. In the 90 days following the expiry of the permit, the foreign national is considered to be without status, by may be able to apply to restore their TR status. However, they cannot trigger the requirements of paragraph R186(u). This means that if the foreign national in Canada does not apply to renew their permit prior to its expiry, while they may be eligible for restoration of status, they may not apply to extend or renew the permit AND they are no longer authorized to work. For more information regarding implied status, go to: [http://cicintranet.ci.gc.ca/connexion/tools-](http://cicintranet.ci.gc.ca/connexion/tools-) outils/temp/visa/validity-validite/implied-implicite-eng.aspx

## Restoration of Status

If a temporary resident in Canada does not apply to extend or renew their work permit, study permit or visitor record prior to expiry, then they are considered to have lost their TR status on the date their permit expired. If a visitor, worker or student has lost their status, they may apply to reinstate or restore their status in accordance

Language

In order to meet the MEC for the FSW program, according to R75(2)(d) of the IRPR, at the time of application, an applicant must identify which of English or French is to be considered their first official language and which is to be considered their second official language, and must be assessed by a designated organization and submit the results of that assessment with their application. The applicant must evaluated against the Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB 7) for English and the Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadien (NCLC 7) for French, and must achieve minimum scores for reading, writing, speaking and listening.

The following test results are acceptable evidence of language proficiency:

IELTS (International English Language Testing System) administered by the British Council, the University of Cambridge and Education Australia; CELPIP (Canadian English Language Proficiency Index Program), administered by the University of British Columbia; TEF (Test d’évaluation du français) administered by Chambre de commerce de Paris (Alliance Française abroad); and TCF Canada: Test de connaissance du français, administered by Centre international d'études pédagogiques (CIEP) for the French Ministry of Education PTE Core: Pearson Test of English, you must take the PTE CORE option

Applicants are only required to submit their test reference number. Language test results are verified by CiO clerks at the time of completeness check. Points are awarded based on equivalency grids.

Language test results must be valid (less than two years old) both when the applicant

completes the Express Entry profile; AND applies for permanent residence

Education Credential Assessments (ECA) Equivalency assessments (ECA reports) will be used as conclusive evidence that the applicant's completed foreign diplomas, certificates or credentials are equivalent to completed Canadian educational credentials. The ECA report will also include an assessment by the organization or institution of the authenticity of the completed foreign diploma, certificate or credential.

Applicants (where applicable) are only required to submit their ECA reference number, not a copy of their assessment. ECA reports are verified by CIO clerks at the time of the completeness check. Applicants must declare in their Express Entry profile if they have obtained an ECA for their foreign educational credential. An ECA report must be less than five years old at the time the Express Entry profile is submitted and upon receipt of the application for permanent residence.

ECA reports are only accepted if the report was issued after the organization was designated as an ECA provided for IRCC. There are 7 designated ECA providers as follows:

## Proof of funds

In order to meet the MEC for the FSW program (R76(1)(b)(i)), FSW applicants are also required to show proof that they have sufficient funds in respect to the number of family members included with the application, whether accompanying or not. It is not necessary to demonstrate this if the applicant has been awarded FSW selection points for having arranged employment as defined in R82 and the MI's. Applicants who have a qualifying offer of arranged employment are exempted from this assessment.

Proof of funds is required, unless the applicant

- is currently able to legally work in Canada
- has a valid job offer from an employer in Canada
The amount of money required is determined by the size of the family. To calculate the size of the family you must include:

PA spouse or common-law partner dependent children of the PA and spouse/CL partner; and dependents of dependent children

Family size includes all family members whether accompanying or non-accompanying. It also includes family members who are permanent residents or Canadian citizens

Funds must be readily available and unencumbered by debt. For example, an applicant can't use equity on real property as proof of settlement funds – they have to have available money. However, if a client provides documentation showing a mortgage or car loan that has a remaining balance, we do not need to subtract what's owing from the amount of available settlement funds, since there is associated equity with these purchases.

The funds must be available, with sufficient liquidity (within 3 months of the time of assessment). The agent should be satisfied that the applicant is able to legally access them to support his/her establishment in Canada on arrival.

For proof, applicants must provide official letters from any banks or financial institutions where they are holding money.

Immigration, Refugees Immigration, Réfugiés and Citizenship Canadaet Citoyenneté Canada L'nformation divulguée en vertu de la toi sur l’accès à Tinformation Qualifying offer of arranged employment

A qualifying offer of arranged employment is defined in subsection 29(2) of the Express Entry Ministerial Instructions. Depending on the immigration program, the term is defined differently.

Under the FSWC, a job offer is considered to be a “qualifying offer of arranged employment" if it is for continuous, paid, full-time work that is, not seasonal, in TEER 0, 1, 2 OR 3 of the National Occupational Classification (NOC) matrix, that is for at least one year after issuance of visa for permanent residence, and if it meets one of the following three conditions:

1. the employer making the job offer has a positive Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) from Employment and Social Development Canada that approves the offer and names the candidate and their position; or
2. the candidate
- is currently working in Canada in a NOC TEER 0, 1, 2 or 3 job on a work permit that was issued based on an LMIA,
- is working for an employer listed on the work permit,
- is authorized to work in Canada when submitting their application and when the visa is issued, and
- has received a job offer from their employer for a full-time job in NOC TEER 0, 1, 2 or 3 for at least one year if accepted as a permanent resident; or
3. the candidate has a valid work permit for a job in NOC TEER 0, 1, 2 or 3 that is exempt from needing an LMIA (under an international agreement such as the North America Free Trade Agreement, a federal- provincial agreement, or other cases supporting Canadian interests) and the candidate:
- is currently working for an employer specified on the work permit
- has accumulated one year of full-time work experience (or an equal amount of part-time work) and
- has a valid job offer from that employer for at least one year after their visa for permanent residence is issued.
REMEMBER: The employer must be named on the LMIA-exempt work permit. An ‘open' work permit would not meet this requirement.

NOTE: Under 3rd condition, LMIA exempt work permit under R204 (a) or (c) or R205.

NOTE: For information on the current Ministerial Instructions, refer to the following website:

[https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/policies-operational-](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/corporate/mandate/policies-operational-) instructions-agreements/ministerial-instructions/express-entry-application-management-system.html

Immigration, Réfugiés and Citizenshi Canada et Ciloyeneé Canada Information disclosed under the Access to Information Act L'information divulguée en vertu de la oi sur l’accès à Finformation Federal skilled workers: Assessing against the selection criteria In order to meet the MEC for the FSW program (R76(2)), FSW applicants are also required to show that they meet the minimum number of points required of a skilled worker.

R76 specifies how to determine whether a skilled worker will be able to become economically established in Canada. This regulation, along with R75, identify the minimum entry criteria (MEC) for a federal skilled worker.

## SELECTION CRITERIA

Six selection factors are set out in R76(1)(a). GCMS will award the applicant points in each of the following areas, based on the information and documents provided in the e-APR: Education Official language proficiency Work experience Age Arranged employment Adaptability

R76(2) allows the Minister to set the “minimum number of points required of a skilled worker" – more commonly known as the “pass mark". The pass mark is currently set at 67 points.

## GCMS procedures

Work through the ADMM and GCMS simultaneously.

## EE ELGIBILITY

1) Go to Assessment tab and highlight the latest Candidate line.
2) Ensure the CRS score is minimum score or greater and that FSW MEC shows MET.
a) If FSW MEC = NOT MET; refer to the following 11.2 Decision section.
# 3) Watch for changes in the scores between ITA and REVISED columns.

# 4) Go to Employment tab; click [W/E Multipull] on ADMM.

## 5) Watch for part-time hours; Canadian employment during full-time study; Self-employment in Canada.

6) Go to Education tab and compare level of education to CRS points in ADMM
7) Watch for Canadian study.
# 8) Go to Job offer tab if CRS points awarded for Arranged Employment.

a) Note the employer; job position; LMIA # if any; Snag-it is helpful at this point.
9) Go to the Language tab to determine the lowest CLB level for the PA. (This is helpful when assessing the Skill Transferability Factors; CLB 7 vs CLB 9)
### GCMS NOTES

## 10) Go to NOTES view.

11) Review the R10 notes to confirm the language and education documents were verified at R10.
### CORRESPONDENCE-INCOMING

12) Go to Correspondence -Incoming and sort the items in alphabetical order.
13) Review Birth certificates for any children.
14) Review Client Information (or Client Enquiry) for any information relevant to the 11.2 decision.
15) Review the PA's and SP/CLP's Education documents and ensure the CRS points were awarded correctly (compare to ADMM). Note any discrepancies for correction/adjustments later.
16) Review the PA's Employment documents for foreign work experience and any Canadian work to ensure the CRS points were awarded correctly. Toggle on ADMM under CRS Points and FSW tabs as applicable. Note any discrepancies in ADMM for correction/adjustments later.
17) Review the Funds item to ensure supporting documents are provided. Determine the equivalent in Canadian dollars. If unable to verify the required level of funds, note the eDoc # in ADMM and set the item to “Review Required". Leave the A11.2 decision as “Review Required” and add an appropriate Summary Note in the ADMM.
## 18) Review any Offer of Employment items, if applicable. Note as applicable in ADMM.

19) Review the Marriage Certificate or Stat Dec of CL Union, if applicable. (Watch for possible marriage of convenience, etc.) Same for divorce certs.
20) Review any other items marked as “Review Required" for any information relevant to the 11.2 decision.
21) Review any "Provided" items. Change Status to "Received" & change Review Status as applicable:
a) Change the Status to "Received".
b) Change the Review Status to:

23) Check FOSS/Integrated Search for any adverse information.

EE ELGIBILITY

28) Make any necessary adjustments/corrections to Employment or Education records.
a) Copy the record; make necessary corrections and save; mark the incorrect record “Rejected"
29) Return to the Assessment tab.
a) On the 11.2-EE MI line, “Calculate" and [Alt] [Enter] until Status reads “Review Required"
b) Confirm FSW MEC show MET and CRS score is minimum score or greater for MET decision.
c) If 11.2 decision is MET, change Status from “Review Required" to “Met"
d) If 11.2 decision requires review by Officer, leave status as “Review Required"
e) If 11.2 decision is NOT MET, change Status from “Review Required” to “Not Met"

## IRPA

Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

Canadian immigration and refugee law concerns the area of law related to the admission of foreign nationals* into Canada, their rights and responsibilities once admitted, and the conditions of their removal. The primary law on these matters is the "Immigration and Refugee Protection Act"(IRPA).

“foreign national” means a person who is not a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident and includes a stateless person. A foreign national may be outside Canada or already in Canada.

“permanent resident” of Canada refers to a person who has acquired resident status under IRPA, and not subsequently lost that status.

The "Immigration and Refugee Protection Act"(IRPA) is an Act of the Parliament of Canada, passed in 2002, and is the primary federal legislation regulating immigration to Canada. It replaced the "Immigration Act” of 1976.

How to read IRPA The legislation is composed of two main parts: The Act and The Regulations. Throughout this manual, references to “the Act” include regulations made under it as well.

IRPA creates a high level framework detailing the goals and guidelines the Canadian governm ent has set with regard to immigration into Canada by foreign residents. The Regulations contain the laws created to fit within the IRPA in order to specify how the IRPA is to be applied.

Sections of IRPA are commonly preceded by an “A” (ie. A12), whereas sections of the Regulations are commonly preceded by an “R” (ie. R70).

Objectives and Application

Some main objectives of this Act with respect to immigration are:

- to permit Canada to pursue the maximum social, cultural and economic benefits of immigration;
- to see that families are reunited in Canada;
- to protect public health and safety and to maintain the security of Canadian society;
- to promote international justice and security by fostering respect for human rights and by denying access to Canadian territory to persons who are criminals or security risks; and
- to offer safe haven to persons with a well-founded fear of persecution based on race, religion, nationality, political opinion or membership in a particular social group, as well as those at risk of torture or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment;

This Act is to be applied in a manner that:

## (a) furthers the domestic and international interests of Canada;

(b) promotes accountability and transparency by enhancing public awareness of immigration and refugee programs;

(c) facilitates cooperation between the Government of Canada, provincial governments, foreign states, international organizations and non-governmental organizations;

(d) ensures that decisions taken under this Act are consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, including its principles of equality and freedom from discrimination and of the equality of English and French as the official languages of Canada;

(e) supports the commitment of the Government of Canada to enhance the vitality of the English and French linguistic minority communities in Canada; and

(f) complies with international human rights instruments to which Canada is signatory.

Permanent Residents

IRPA provides the rules by which a foreign national can be deemed inadmissible or denied entry to Canada; be admitted to Canada on a temporary basis; obtain status in Canada as a Permanent Resident; maintain their status in Canada; and more. The following section highlights some important sections of the act and regulations.

Requirements Before Entering Canada A11. (1) A foreign national must, before entering Canada, apply to an officer for a visa or for any other document required by the regulations. The visa or document may be issued if, following an examination, the officer is satisfied that the foreign national is not inadmissible and meets the requirements of this Act.

A16. (1) A person who makes an application must answer truthfully all questions put to them for the purpose of the examination and must produce a visa and all relevant evidence and documents that the officer reasonably requires.

A18. (1) Every person seeking to enter Canada must appear for an examination to determine whether that person has a right to enter Canada or is or may become authorized to enter and remain in Canada.

Upon Entry

## A20. (1) Every foreign national who seeks to enter or remain in Canada must establish,

(a) to become a permanent resident, that they hold the visa or other document required under the regulations and have come to Canada in order to establish permanent residence; and
(b) to become a temporary resident, that they hold the visa or other document required under the regulations and will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay
A21. (1) A foreign national becomes a permanent resident if an officer is satisfied that the foreign national has applied for that status, has met the obligations set out in paragraph 20(1)(a) and subsection 20(2) and is not inadmissible.

Dual intent

(2) An intention by a foreign national to become a permanent resident does not preclude them from becoming a temporary resident if the officer is satisfied that they will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay. Right of permanent residents A27. (1) A permanent resident of Canada has the right to enter and remain in Canada, subject to the provisions of this Act. A28. (1) A permanent resident must comply with a residency obligation with respect to every five-year period. Page |8CEC 11.2 TRAINING MANUAL APR2021CIO Sydney

## Economic Class

A12(2) A foreign national may be selected as a member of the economic class on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada.

One of the three Classes of immigration and permanent residence is the Economic Class, which includes applicants who will be assessed on the skills and/or expertise they could bring to Canada. The economic

# permanent resident applicants are assessed against a selection system based on a category. These categories

are:

- Federal skilled worker Quebec skilled worker
- Provincial nominee
- Canadian Experience Federal Skilled Trades
- Start-Up Business
- Atlantic Immigration Pilot Program
- Immigrant Investor Venture Capital Class
- Rural and Northern Immigration Program
- Business applicants: Entrepreneur Investor Self-employed
- Quebec Business
## 1. Federal Skilled Worker (FSW)

This program is designed for applicants who are skilled workers, who may become permanent residents on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada, and who intend to reside in a province other than Quebec. Successful applicants must have a minimum of one year of “skilled” work

# experience and meet the minimum requirements for education, language abilities as well as other

# requirements to demonstrate their ability to successfully establish themselves in Canada.

## 2. Quebec Skilled Worker (QSW)

Persons who are destined to become permanent residents in Quebec are assessed under the Quebec skilled worker class and must meet Quebec's selection criteria to be eligible.

# If they are successful, they will receive an appropriate Certificate of Selection of Quebec (CSQ).

Nonetheless, these applicants also need to meet the federal requirements for admissibility. If they fail to

# meet either provincial eligibility or federal admissibility, their applications will be refused.

3. Provincial nominee (PNP)
## Another type of independent permanent resident applicant is a provincial nominee. Applicants under this

category are selected in consultation with the province interested in making the nomination. In some

# cases provinces will seek to nominate applicants with experience in occupations considered “in demand”

## within that province. Applicants holding a provincial nomination must also meet federal requirements for

admissibility.

4. Canadian Experience (CEC) The Canadian Experience Class is prescribed as a class of persons who may become permanent residents on the basis of their Canadian experience and who:
- intend to reside in a province or territory other than Quebec;
- have acquired a minimum of one year work experience in Canada; have maintained temporary resident status during their qualifying period of work experience in Canada; and
- meet the language requirement.
5. Federal Skilled Trades (FST) The Federal Skilled Trades Program is for people who want to become permanent residents based on being qualified in a skilled trade. To apply, you must have work experience in a specific skilled trade and meet several other requirements.
6. Start-Up Business Class (SUBC) The Start Up Business Program is for people who may become permanent residents on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada as innovative business persons. In order to be eligible, a person must have a Commitment Certificate issued by a designated entity. Once an applicant provides proof of having a commitment from a designated entity other factors will be reviewed and assessed against the Ministerial Instructions for selection and admissibility.
# 7. Atlantic Immigration Pilot Program (AIPP)

The Atlantic Immigration Pilot is for foreign nationals who have the ability to become economically established in Atlantic Canada, intend to reside in a province in the Atlantic region, and meet all of the

## following pass or fail criteria: Provincial endorsement; minimum education requirements; minimum

language proficiency requirements; minimum work experience within the 3 years before the date of application; minimum job offer requirements.

### The Process:

# Economic Class applications for permanent residence are submitted to the Centralized Intake Office at CPC-

Sydney in Nova Scotia. The ClO checks the application for completeness, creates the application in the electronic database, and process the payment. In some cases CiO completes the assessment and finalizes the application for permanent residence. More complex cases are forwarded to other offices in the Domestic, International or Centralized Network for continued processing. Triage criteria have been developed to determine which applications are referred to other offices, and at which stage of processing the referral will take place.

After meeting specific eligibility criteria for the particular program as described above, all applicants still need to be admissible in order to be granted the status of Permanent Resident. Generally this would include a medical screening and background checks for criminality and security. Once all members of the family meet all requirements, each individual is issued a permanent resident visa that is processed when they arrive in Canada.

Traditionally, all of our applications were received on paper via Canada Post or courier. Since January 2015 we now have another system for managing application intake. Applicants can now go online and submit their Page|13CEC 11.2 TRAINING MANUAL APR2021CIO Sydney

This is a faster, easier way for the applicants to submit their application, once they have been invited to apply. There are also benefits for our department which we will talk about throughout the training.

There are several Economic Class programs which are eligible for processing under EE, including: Federal Skilled Workers, Canadian Experience Class, Federal Skilled Trades, and certain Provincial Nominees.

Section 11.2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) includes a new authority that supports the Express Entry system, and adds a new level of decision making for permanent residence applications. Under A11.2, we are able to refuse an EE application when the applicant does not meet minimum entry criteria (MEC) or did not or does not possess the qualifications for which they received their invitation to apply.

The 11.2 decisions for Federal Skilled Worker applications will be the focus of this training. In the next module you will be introduced to some key concepts related to the Express Entry application management system, and look at both the requirement to maintain the MEC, and the requirement to prove and maintain the self- declared qualifications for which they were awarded points resulting in the invitation to apply.

### Introduction to Express Entry

## Express Entry is an application management system. It is a method of ranking potential immigration

candidates, choosing those with the highest qualifications and inviting them to apply for permanent residence.

# Candidates, or potential applicants, get the benefit of more efficient processing and accelerated processing

times. For IRCC, it is a way for our department to better manage the intake of economic class applications and

## prevent backlogs (at least at the intake stage), while providing consistent, efficient processing for applicants.

Candidates create an online Express Entry profile in their MyCIC account and, if invited to apply, submit their application for permanent residence (APR) through their MyCIC account.

Express Entry POOL

Application Express Entry 1 – MINIMUM ENTRY CRITERIA 2 – COMPREHENSIVE SubmissionAND POINTS SCORE RANKING SYSTEM3 - INVITATION TO APPLYfor permanent résidence

### Business Process

Foreign nationals who are interested in living in Canada permanently and who have work experience in a skilled occupation, may register and create a personal secure online account in with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada. During this process, potential applicants (Candidates) will enter information related to their: Age Level of education Language abilities Work experience Family members Details related to any job offers in Canada

The system will determine whether the foreign national meets the Minimum Entry Criteria (MEC) for any of the eligible programs for Express Entry processing, and assign a value to each applicable aspect according to the MEC.

When a candidate's profile shows that they meet the minimum entry criteria (MEC), the system automatically enters their profile into the Express Entry pool. Potential candidates MUST meet the criteria for one of the programs set up for EE in order to get into the pool. Candidates receive a notification letting them know when their profile has been placed in the EE pool, and that their profile will remain in the pool for 365 days. This notification gives the candidate their score and ranking as well as detailed instructions for next steps, including instruction to begin gathering documents to support the

claims they have made when creating their profile. While in the pool, the candidate may update their profile at any time.

The message also gives them their Express Entry profile number and a Job Seeker validation code, which are automatically generated by the system. Candidates need their Job Seeker validation code to register for the Government of Canada's Job Bank, an electronic listing of jobs provided by employers from across Canada. Candidates without a job offer or a provincial or territorial nomination will be required to register with the Job Bank to complete and submit their Express Entry profile. Express Entry candidates can be matched with Canadian employers and jobs based on their skills, knowledge and experience.

At this point, the candidate is eligible to receive an Invitation to Apply (ITA) for the program whose requirements they appear to meet. A specific number of invitations are issued (ITA) on a regular, usually bi- weekly basis, to Express Entry candidates who have the highest Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) scores at the time of an Express Entry round of invitations. Those who receive an ITA have 60 days to apply. This deadline is indicated in the client's correspondence, which they can access in their MyCIC account. Candidates who are issued an ITA have three options: they can respond to the ITA; they can ignore it (in which case they are removed from the Express Entry pool); they can decline it, in which case they return to the pool for

## consideration in future rounds of invitations. Candidates may ONLY apply for permanent residence online if

they receive an invitation to apply through the Express Entry system. Completing an online Express Entry profile or entering the pool doesn't guarantee that a candidate will be invited to apply for permanent residence.

A foreign national is considered to be a “CANDIDATE" up until he/she submits an application for permanent residence (APR). Once an application is submitted he/she is considered to be an “APPLICANT".

### Comprehensive Ranking System

The Comprehensive Ranking System, or CRS, is a points-based system used to assess and score a candidate's Express Entry profile and determine a candidate's position in the Express Entry pool. It ranks prospective skilled immigrants by looking at their skills, work experience, language ability, education and other factors that we know lead to success in Canada. Each candidate in the Express Entry pool is ranked according to points awarded for certain economic selection factors. A candidate's total score is known as the CRS score.

According to A10.3(1) and A87.3(3), the minister may give instructions with respect to the way immigration

# applications are processed. From time to time such Ministerial Instructions are released to guide our

# processing, and these instructions should be applied in conjunction with IRPA.

The Express Entry application management system is primarily governed using Ministerial Instructions. Throughout the training we will refer to the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system. We use these Ministerial Instructions to guide us in our decision making, specifically the decisions we make related to A11.2. Further decisions related to program eligibility and ina dmissibility require the application of

# program regulations and other specific sections of IRPA.

As required by IRPA, subsection 10.3(4), all Ministerial Instructions related to Express Entry must be published on IRCC's website. Some Ministerial Instructions must also be posted in the Canada Gazette. The Ministerial
