CRS points and the Ministerial Instructions

According to Section 8 of the Current Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system, the total number of points that may be assigned under the Comprehensive Ranking System is 1200 points, allocated as follows:

•(a) for the core human capital factors

(i) a maximum of 500 points if the foreign national has no accompanying spouse or common-law partner, or 0(ii) a maximum of 460 points if the foreign national has an accompanying spouse or common-law partner;
(b) for accompanying spouse or common-law partner factors, a maximum of 40 points;
(c) for skill transferability factors, a maximum of 100 points; and
(d) for additional factors, a maximum of 600 points.
Comprehensive Ranking System factor categories: Points are assigned under the Comprehensive Ranking System to each foreign national in the express entry pool according to the following categories of factors:

•(a) the category of core human capital factors, namely

(i) age, (ii) level of education, (iii) official language proficiency, and (iv) Canadian work experience;
- (b) the category of accompanying spouse or common-law partner factors, namely
(i) level of education of the spouse or common-law partner, (ii) official language proficiency of the spouse or common-law partner, and (iii) Canadian work experience of the spouse or common-law partner;
•(c) the category of skill transferability factors, namely

(i) the combination of level of education and official language proficiency, (ii) the combination of level of education and Canadian work experience, O(iii) the combination of foreign work experience and official language proficiency, O(iv) the combination of Canadian work experience and foreign work experience, and
(v) the combination of a certificate of qualification and official language proficiency; and
•(d) the category of additional factors, namely

(i) a provincial nomination, (ii) a qualifying offer of arranged employment, (iii) Canadian educational credentials, (iv) a sibling in Canada, and
(v) French-language proficiency.

## CEC Minimum Entry Criteria

Candidates must meet the Minimum Entry Criteria for one of the 3 federal programs eligible for Express Entry processing, in order to receive an invitation to apply. Ministerial Instructions respecting the Expr ess Entry system list the MEC for Express Entry. Applicants must meet the MEC to be accepted into the Express Entry pool and must also meet the MEC when they are issued an ITA and when they submit their e-APR.

The Express Entry system analyzes an applicant's abilities and experience as entered in the candidate's profile, to determine whether the Minimum Entry Criteria have been met for one or more of the 3 federal programs eligible for Express Entry Processing: Federal Skilled Worker, Canadian Experience Class, or Federal Skilled Trades. A Case Processing Agent at the Centralized Intake Office must determine if the applicant actually does meet the MEC for the program in which they were invited to apply, by reviewing all supporting documents and information submitted with the electronic application.

If an applicant's situation changes in the time between when they receive an ITA and when they submit their e- APR to such a degree that their qualifications fall below the MEC, the requirements of A11.2 have not been met and the application must be refused. An officer will need to determine whether the application should be refused for not meeting the minimum requirements of the federal program to which they are applying, or for misrepresentation under section 40 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

Each of the 3 federal programs in Express Entry has their own Minimum Entry Criteria. The MEC for the Canadian Experience Class are:

- Minimum work experience: must have accumulated at least one (1) year full-time, paid, qualifying work experience (or the equivalent part-time experience) within the last three (3) years in Canada, in an occupation or occupations described in NOC 0, A or B of the National Occupational Classification (NOC). In order for work experience to qualify under CEC, during the period of work experience the applicant must:
not be engaged in full-time study; be authorized to work; and have temporary resident status.

- Language ability: must provide evidence that they meet the threshold(s) set by the Minister for language proficiency, in either English or French, for each of the four language skill areas: reading, writing, speaking and listening. Language threshold is determined by the NOC level.

Intent to reside

Applicants will indicate within their Express Entry application where they intend to reside when they become a permanent resident. Applicants who indicate an intention to reside in the province of Quebec are not eligible to apply under the CEC program. If you have concerns about the applicant's intention to reside in a province other than Quebec, the file should be referred to an officer for review. Keep in mind that an applicant's experience (either prior or current) in a province does not necessarily denote an intention to live there in the future.

## Qualifying Work Experience

In order to determine whether an applicant meets minimum entry criteria (MEC) for the Canadian Experience Class, a Case Processing Agent must examine whether the requirements of the NOC have been met for work in

# Canada; whether work experience is authorized under a work permit or another regulatory authority; and

whether the applicant has the required TR status. According to R87.1, work experience requirements include:

Work experience must be gained within Canada 1 year in the 3 years prior to APR Full-time work* (or equivalent in part time) Any occupation, or combination of one or more occupations – NOC 0, A and B levels Actions in the lead statement of the NOC; Substantial number of the main duties of the NOC Periods of self-employment may NOT be counted Periods of work during full-time study (including co-op program) may NOT be counted

Work must be authorized under a work permit or other regulatory authority Applicant must maintain valid TR status during the period(s) of work experience

Note: The A11.2 assessment also includes an evaluation and calculation of CRS points, as with all applications submitted

## A11.2 Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

Visa or other document not to be issued

11.2 (1) An officer may not issue a visa or other document in respect of an application for permanent
residence to a foreign national who was issued an invitation to make that application if— at the time the invitation was issued or at the time the officer received their application — the foreign national did not meet the criteria set out in an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1) (e) or did not have the qualifications on the basis of which they were ranked under an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1) (h) and were issued the invitation.

Exceptions

(2) Despite subsection (1), an officer may issue the visa or other document if, at the time the officer received their application,
(a) the foreign national did not meet the criteria set out in an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1) (e) or did not have the qualifications on the basis of which they were ranked under an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1) (h) — because the applicant's birthday occurred after the invitation was issued; or
(b) the foreign national did not have the qualifications they had at the time the invitation was issued and on the basis of which they were ranked under an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1) (h), but
(i) they met the criteria set out in an instruction given under paragraph 10.3(1) (e), and (ii) they occupied a rank that is not lower than the rank that a foreign national was
required to have occupied to be invited to make an application.

According to A11.2 when reviewing an application, processing offices must determine if

- the applicant possesses the qualifications that they declared in their e-APR, as corroborated by the applicant's supporting documentation; and when the applicant submits their e-APR, the information provided in their Express Entry profile has not materially changed to the degree that the applicant would not have been issued an ITA in that round of invitations.
Processing offices must compare the information in the applicant's profile at the time of the round of invitations to the information in their e-APR to ensure that the applicant meets the requirements of

## section A11.2. Note that not all discrepancies should result in a refusal (A11.2(2)).

### Requirement to maintain the MEC

A11.2 specifies that applicants must meet the criteria set out in A10.3(e) to be accepted into the Express Entry pool and must also meet this criteria when they are issued an ITA and when they submit their e-APR.

10.3 (1) The Minister may give instructions governing any matter relating to the application of this Division,
including instructions respecting (e) the criteria that a foreign national must meet to be eligible to be invited to make an application;

The criteria referred to in this subsection is otherwise known as the "Minimum Entry Criteria" for the program in which the applicant is applying. Ministerial Instructions for Express Entry list the Minimum Entry Criteria (MEC) for each program (s.2 and s.5). If you determine that the applicant did not meet the MEC for the program at the time he/she was invited to apply, the application should be refused. If an applicant's situation changes in the time between when they receive an ITA and when they submit their e-APR to such a degree that they no longer meet the MEC, the application must be refused under section A11.2. An officer will need to consider whether the application should be refused for not meeting the minimum requirements of the

## federal program to which they are applying, or for misrepresentation (A40).

### Requirement to maintain the CRS score

A11.2 also specifies that an applicant must have the qualifications described in 10.3(1)(h) of IRPA at the time they are issued the invitation to apply and at the time the application is received.

10.3 (1) The Minister may give instructions governing any matter relating to the application of this Division,
including instructions respecting (h) the basis on which an eligible foreign national may be ranked relative to other eligible foreign nationals

The name of the system or basis on which EE candidates are ranked is the “Comprehensive Ranking System". Candidates are awarded a score for each of their self-declared qualifications. These scores are totaled and amount to the candidate's CRS score. When a round of invitations occurs, IRCC invites the top-ranked candidates in the Express Entry pool to apply for permanent residence. After each round of invitations, IRCC publishes the score of the lowest-ranked candidate to receive an ITA in that round of invitations.

An applicant's CRS score is automatically recorded in GCMS at the time when

- their ITA is issued; and
- their e-APR is submitted.
Applicants are required to maintain the qualifications that led them to be included in the top-ranked candidates to be issued an ITA in a particular round of invitations. At the time of the e-APR, processing officers should compare both CRS scores to determine which of the following scenarios should be applied:

- If the applicant's CRS score at the time of the e-APR is equal to or higher than the lowest-ranked score in the round of invitations, the application will not be refused under section A11.2, as long as the applicant's supporting documentation corroborates their claims and they continue to meet the MEC for Express Entry, including the requirements of the program to which they were invited to apply. - If the applicant's CRS score at the time of the e-APR is lower than the lowest-ranked score in the round of invitations, the application should be refused under section A11.2 for not having maintained the qualifications that would justify the ITA. The main exception to this is those applicants who lost points because they had a birthday between ITA and the submission of their e-APR –see the example scenario below.

Ministerial Instructions related to the CRS are revised periodically. Applications must be assessed under section A11.2 according to the Ministerial Instructions in force during the round of invitations to which the candidate is invited. In other words, an applicant's CRS score at the time of the ITA and at the time of application should be calculated based on the Ministerial Instructions in place at the time of the ITA.

Exemption to section A11.2(1): candidates whose birthday occurs after they receive an ITA

An applicant may have a birthday after they receive an ITA but before they submit their e-APR. Their change in age may lower their CRS score below the lowest score in the round of invitations, resulting in a refusal based on section A11.2.

When a change in age results in having the recalculated CRS points score fall below the lowest points score in

# that round of invitations, processing offices will apply the exemption in A11.2(2).

Example scenario: candidate has a birthday between ITA and e-APR

Jan is 35 years old when she receives her ITA. She has met the MEC for CEC and CRS points are above the minimum cut-off score at ITA. Between her ITA and e-APR, Jan turns 36. Due to her change in age, Jan's CRS score drops by 5 points, putting her below the lowest-ranked candidate in her round of invitations.

You will grant Jan the exemption and, consequently, Jan continues to meet the MEC/CRS score for A11.2. This exempts Jan from being refused under section A11.2 for her adjusted CRS score and for not meeting program requirements.

IRPA defines the classes in which foreign nationals can apply to immigrate to Canada, and requirements for

individual's ability to become economically established (Selection); and grounds for inadmissibility to Canada

All programs included in Express Entry fall under the Economic Class. The Economic Class is generally prescribed as a class of persons who are skilled workers, who may become permanent residents on the basis of

## their ability to become economically established in Canada. Ministerial Instructions for Express Entry (s.2)

## defer to the specific sections of IRPR, for program criteria for each federal program:

(b) the Canadian experience class referred to in subsection 87.1(1) of the Regulations;
(c) the federal skilled trades class referred to in subsection 87.2(2) of the Regulations; and
(d) members of the provincial nominee class referred to in subsection 87(2) of the Regulations who are nominated by the government of one of the following provinces under its provincial nominee program express entry stream
The Canadian Experience Class is for applicants who intend to reside in a province other than Quebec, and who have gained work experience IN CANADA in an occupation at the 0, A or B skill level. The Minimum Entry Criteria (MEC) required for CEC are:

Introduction to the NOC and NOC Matrix

NOC The National Occupational Classification (NOC) is the nationally accepted reference on occupations in Canada. It is used analyze and communicate information about occupations, and to understand the jobs found throughout Canada's labour market. The NOC is a standard that classifies and describes the occupations in the Canadian economy.

### NOC Matrix

The NOC Matrix provides an overview of the entire occupational classification structure for jobs in Canada, based on Skill Levels and Broad Occupational Categories or Types of occupations. Skill Levels are represented in the columns while the Skill Types are found in rows. Senior Management and other Managerial occupations are found in the first column of the chart, indicating the presence of management across all segments of the labour market.

The occupational categories (except Management) are displayed in rows and are represented by numbers zero (0) to nine (9) while the skill levels are displayed in columns and are identified by letters A to D. Managerial occupations, which are considered as skill level A occupations, are found on the left-end side of the chart, indicating the presence of management across all segments of the labour market.

For most economic class programs the requirement is that the work must be in the Skill Type 0 (Management), or Skill levels A or B.

### Skill Types / Occupational Categories

0 Management occupations 00 Senior management occupations 01-09 Middle management occupations in various fields 1 Business, finance and administration occupations 2 Natural and applied sciences and related occupations

## 3 Health occupations

4 Occupations in education, law and social, community and government services

Skill Level A: Professional Occupations, Usually Requiring a University Education Always have "0” or “1” as the second digit. For skill level A, the first digit will identify the skill type.

Example: NOC 3112: General Practitioners and Family Physicians 1 as the second digit indicates skill level A; 3 as the first digit indicates Heath Occupations (type).

Skill Level B: Technical, Usually Require College Education/Apprenticeship Training Will have “2” or “3” as the second digit. For skill level B, as with skill level A, the first digit will identify the skill type.

Example: NOC 6321:Chefs 3 as the second digit indicates skill level B; 6 as the first digit indicates Sales and Service Occupations (type).

Skill Level C: Occupations Usually Require High School plus Job-Specific Training Will have “4” or "5” as the second digit. For skill level C, as with skill levels A and B, the first digit will identify the skill type.

Example: NOC 7511: Transport Truck Drivers 5 as the second digit indicates skill level C; 7 as the first digit indicates Trades and Transport Occupations (type).

Skill Type "0": Management Occupations: High Level of Responsibility With all other A and B skill level occupations, you need to pay attention to the second digit to identify the skill level. For Management occupations this rule changes. NOC codes at the management level will always begin with a "0”, so they are easily identified. For most management occupations, the second digit (1 through 9) corresponds to management within each Skill Type. *Exception: When the second digit is also zero, this represents "senior" management occupations. Example: NOC 0631: Restaurant and Food Services Managers 0 indicates Management Occupation (level), 6 indicates Sales and Service Occupations (type)

### Reviewing the NOC website:

Each NOC description includes the following elements:

Lead Statement The lead statement provides a general description of the occupation and the boundaries of the unit group. It also indicates the kinds of industries, workplaces or establishments where the occupation is found. Applicants must have performed the actions in the lead statement in order to include the period of work experience in the stated NOC.

Example Titles Example titles are the occupational titles commonly found within the group. This list is an extraction of a more expansive listing of alphabetical job titles found in the NOC Index of Titles. The example titles may help to determine if the work experience is in the stated NOC.

Main Duties The main duties section describes the most significant duties of the occupations in the group. Depending on the Unit Group, it may include:

- a series of statements that can be applied to all occupations in the group;
- two or more sub-sets of occupations with statements that apply to each sub-set or component; and/or
- a series of brief statements that are linked to specific occupations, that, while similar enough to be in the same group, can be described separately.
Statements in Italics, at the end of this section, identify a specialization that may exist within the occupation.

Note that there are times when employment duties overlap from one unit group to another (ie. 3012 Registered Nurse and 3413 Nursing Assistant). An assessment of job duties must include consideration of the duties that are most important for the particular occupation. In many cases it is not enough to determine that half or more than half of the listed duties have been performed by the applicant. Duties are organized and listed according to significance to the job – most prominent or important duties are listed first. If the

## statement begins with “may perform", the duty is not critical to that occupation.

### Employment Requirements

# Employment requirements are prerequisites generally needed to enter the occupation. Several types of

requirements are listed: •type and level of education including specific subject matter if relevant, starting with the lowest possible requirement for entry into the occupation;

- specific training required, including apprenticeship, on-the-job or internal training;
- experience in a related occupation, especially for supervisory or managerial occupations;
### licences, certificates or affiliations; and/or

- other requirements not dependent on formal education, such as athletic abilities, artistic talent or presentation of a portfolio.
While some occupations have very specific employment requirements, others have a wide range of acceptable requirements. The following terminology is used to indicate the level of the requirement:

### •"Is required" indicates a definite requirement.

- "Is usually required" means that the qualification is generally expressed as required by a majority of employers, but not always mandatory.
- "May be required" describes requirements that some employers may impose, but are not universal.
*Note – for CEC, it is not necessary that the employment requirements be met; the regulations specify must have performed lead statement and main duties.

### Qualifying Work Experience

## "Status" and “authorization” are separate in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). Work

included to meet the MEC for CEC must be authorized work, and it must be performed while the applicant has valid TR status. It is possible for a foreign national to be authorized to work and not have TR status. Likewise, it is possible for a foreign national to have TR status and not be authorized to perform work.

Under IRPA, all foreign nationals authorized to enter Canada as per A22(1) have temporary resident status. A temporary resident may also be authorized to work in Canada without a work permit [R186] or be issued a work permit [R200 or R201].

Definition of “work” [R2] “Work” is defined in the Regulations as an activity for which wages are paid or commission is earned, or that competes directly with activities of Canadian citizens or permanent residents in the Canadian labour market

# [R2].

Authorized Work Work may be authorized for foreign nationals in Canada either with a work permit, or through another regulatory authority. Work permits may be issued to either visa-required or visa-exempt foreign nationals. Work permits may be employer-driven, based on a Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA), or they may be LMlA-exempt. Some temporary residents may be authorized to work without a work permit in certain

### situations. Keep in mind that work experience gained through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits

while a full-time student and on-campus work permits, does not meet the requirements for CEC. Whether work is performed with or without a work permit, you must ensure both that the work period was authorized

## AND that the foreign national held temporary resident status at the time.

#### Employee vs. self-employed

In determining whether an applicant under the CEC was an employee or a self-employed individual during their period of qualifying work experience in Canada, you should consider factors such as: Page|33CEC 11.2 TRAINING MANUAL APR2021CIO Sydney

- the degree of the worker's control or autonomy in terms of how and when work is performed, and the method(s) used to do the work; whether the worker owns and/or provides tools and equipment to accomplish the work; the degree to which the worker has to perform the work personally and whether the worker has the option of subcontracting work or hiring others to help and assist with completing the work; the degree of financial risk assumed by the worker, including whether the worker is required to make any investment in order to complete the work or provide the service and whether the worker is free to make business decisions that affect his/her ability to realize a profit or incur a loss (as opposed to the opportunity to earn commissions or other productivity bonuses); and any other relevant factors, such as written contracts.

Additional details regarding each of the above factors, and indicators that can be used when determining whether an individual is an employee or self-employed, are available in the Employee or Self-employed? CRA guide.

Determination of the degree of control can be difficult when examining the employment of professionals such as

## engineers, physicians and information technology consultants. Given their expertise and specialized training, they may

need little or no specific direction in their daily activities. When examining the factor of control, it is necessary to focus on both the payer's control over the worker's daily activities, and the payer's influence over the worker. There are also certain occupations in which individuals may be either self-employed or in an employer-employee relationship depending on the specific circumstances of their employment. More information on the determination of a worker's employment status for a number of specific employment categories is available on the CRA website.

Generally speaking, consultants/contractors are considered to be self-employed individuals in a “contract for services" business relationship. For example, independent contractors in the financial, real estate and business service industries. Similarly, individuals who hold substantial ownership and/or exercise management control of a business for which they are also employed are generally considered to be self-employed.

Each application under the CEC is to be considered on its own merits, with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision. No one piece of evidence substantiating work experience is to be taken as “conclusive" evidence. The final decision as to the employment status of the applicant for the purposes of meeting CEC requirements rests with the officer at6 the time of assessment. If you have concerns that the applicant may be self-employed and you are unable to make a determination on your own, refer the file to program support.

website. Full-time work experience means working at least 30 paid hours per week.

Part-time work may be included as long as the applicant has gained the equivalent amount of experience as someone who worked full-time for at least one year (1560 hours).

Work experience does not need to be continuous to qualify, but the period of 12 months of required employment does not include any extended breaks in employment, periods of unemployment, prolonged sickness or parental leave. An allowance for a reasonable period of vacation time will generally be made in calculating the period of qualifying work experience (e.g., a two-week period of paid vacation leave within a given 52-week period in which the applicant was engaged in qualifying work experience). An allowance for normal vacation time during a period of qualifying work experience cannot be used as a substitute or proxy for meeting the in-Canada element of the work experience requirement (i.e. work experience obtained outside Canada will not be considered as though the applicant had been on a period of vacation in order to be counted as part of the period of in-Canada work experience). While officers will account for a reasonable period of vacation time in calculating the period of qualifying work experience in Canada, each application is considered on its own merits with a final decision based on a review of all the information available to the officer at the time of decision.

During the period of employment, an officer must be satisfied that the applicant “performed the actions described in the lead statement for the occupation(s); and “performed a substantial number of the main duties of the occupation(s)”. Any period of employment when the applicant was engaged in full-time study will not be included in calculating the period of qualifying work experience (ie. work through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits while a full-time student and on-campus work permits). Officers should verify the work permit information in GCMS to ensure there are no concerns.

Principal applicants are requested to provide documentary evidence of their work experience in Canada through a combination of: a copy of their most recent work permit (unless they are work-permit exempt), copies of their most recent T4 tax information slips and Notice of Assessment (NOA) issued by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) or a sufficient combination of other supporting documentation, and employer letters of reference for all periods of qualifying work experience claimed in the application.

# Canadian employers are responsible for deducting and remitting Canada Pension Plan (CPP) contributions,

Employment Insurance (EI) premiums, and income tax from remuneration or other amounts they pay to their employees to the CRA. They must also provide employees with a record of their remuneration and deductions in the form of a T4 tax information slip. The T4 slip is therefore key documentary evidence for the vast majority of CEC applicants to demonstrate that they were in an employer-employee work relationship during their period of qualifying work experience in Canada.

However, there is no obligation under the regulations that CEC applicants provide a T4 tax information slip or NOA specifically with their application, and these particular documents cannot be considered conclusive evidence or the only evidence accepted for the purposes of substantiating whether an applicant has qualifying Canadian work experience. As such, in the absence of a T4 tax information slip or NOA, documents which may help substantiate the applicant's work experience in Canada could include a record or letter of employment from the Canadian employer, work contracts and pay stubs.

In all cases, the onus is on the applicant to establish that they meet the CEC program criteria at the time of their application. All applicants are required to provide satisfactory evidence of their work experience in Canada, including the fact that they were in an employer-employee relationship during their period of qualifying work experience.

Work Permits Conditions

Work permits are always issued with conditions. Specific conditions related to temporary work are imposed by an officer and are specific to the client's situation. It is important you understand the imposed conditions such as:

a period of authorized stay the type of work the employer location of work times and period of work

Period of authorized stay A work permit will always indicate the period authorized for stay in Canada (ie. Expiry date). The authorized period of stay may be longer than the authorized period of work [R185(a) and R185(b)(iv)].

Type of work There are a variety of situations where the type of work/occupation is restricted. There are employer-specific work permits and also “open" employer work permits that are occupation-restricted [R185(b)(i)]. Employer-specific work permits are issued for foreign nationals to work in a specific occupation, for a specific employer. These work permits are employer-driven, where the employer must apply for and receive an LMIA* before the foreign national can apply for a work permit, or must issue an offer of employment for LMIA-exempt workers [R204-R208]. "Open" restricted work permit: Where the employer is not listed, a location and/or occupation may be restricted. An occupation may be restricted due to medical or program requirements. For example, the person may not be able to work in jobs where the protection of the public health is required, if they have been assessed as M2, M3, or M4. *LMIA: Labour Market Impact Assessment, or an assessment — provided to the officer by the Department of Employment and Social Development that the requirements set out in subsection 203(1) with respect to the offer have been met

The employer Work permits issued under R200(1)(c)(ii.1) will identify the employer. The employer name will match the employer named on the LMIA or the offer of employment. When an officer issues an employer-specific work permit under an LMIA exemption, GCMS will automatically insert the employer's name into the “Employer” field.

Location of work Location of work must be imposed as a condition where an LMIA has been issued or where it is a requirement of the LMIA exemption [R185(b)(iii)]. For example, when an employer has several franchise locations but indicates only one location on the offer of employment, the work permit should reflect the physical location of work and restrict the work to that location. However, if the employer indicates in the offer of employment that the worker will be working at multiple work locations, the officer should not restrict the work permit to a single location and should indicate in the “Remarks" field that the worker is authorized to work at the various locations across Canada. For LMlA-

Page |37CEC 11.2 TRAINING MANUAL APR2021CIO Sydney

A-2025-58066-000509

Immigration, Refugees Immigration, Réfugiés 中and Citizenship Canada et Citoyenneté Canada L'nformation divulguée en vertu de la toi sur l’accès à Tinformation

supported work permits, the location of work must match the destination on the LMIA. For LMIA-exempt work permits, if the location of work is important to the exemption (such as for provincial nominees), then the location will be specified and the restriction on location imposed.

Times and periods of work While the period of authorized stay may extend beyond the authorization period of work, the period of work may never extend beyond the duration specified in the LMIA or offer of employment. There may also be conditions where worker is not authorized to work at specific times or dates. For example, seasonal

## agricultural workers are never to work between December 15 and January 1; students are automatically

authorized to work for up to 20 hours per week in their off-campus employment during the semester.

## Post-graduation work permit (PGWP): LMIA-exemption code C43

Post-graduation work permits are exempt from Labour Market Impact Assessments. They are considered “open” work permits, and are coded in GCMS as C43. With a post-graduation work permit, as with all open work permits, graduates can work full time, work part time, or be self-employed. A post-graduation work permit may be issued based on the length of the study program for a minimum of 8 months up to a maximum of 3 years. When determining the length of a post-graduation work permit, officers may consider the duration of the program of study in Canada. When assessing work performed while under a PGWP, officers should assess carefully to ensure that the NOC requirements are met, and that the applicant was not self-employed.

Bridging Work permit (BOWP): LMIA-exemption code A75

## Requirements for a bridging open WP are: √ they are currently in Canada;

they have valid status on a work permit that is due to expire in four months or less; they are the principal applicant on an application for permanent residence under FSW, CEC, FST, or PNP

they have received a positive eligibility assessment on their permanent residence application under one of the Economic Class programs above (EE: passed A11.2 decision)

Validity period for work permits When determining the validity period of a work permit, officers must first consider the passport validity. A foreign national must hold a passport that is valid for the period authorized for their stay [R52(1)], unless the applicant is exempted (such as U.S. nationals). A work permit cannot be extended beyond the validity of the passport, as doing so would be putting the temporary worker in a position of non-compliance. [Exceptions to

## this are noted in subsection R52(2)].

As long as the passport is still valid, a work permit will be issued for the complete duration of the LMIA. For LMIA-exempt job offers, the work permit is issued for the expected duration of employment and in some

If a temporary resident visa is necessary, it should have the same duration as the work permit (or passport, if it will expire first), and it should allow for multiple entries where possible. For initial or renewed work permits for visa-exempt foreign nationals: An electronic travel authorization (eTA) will be issued automatically with the work permit. It will be valid for 5 years from the date of issuance or until the client's passport expires (whichever comes first), regardless of whether this date is beyond the expiry date for the work permit.

Working while engaged in full-time study Any period of employment when the applicant was engaged in full-time study cannot be included in calculating the period of qualifying work experience (e.g., work experience gained through co-op work permits, off-campus work permits while a full-time student and on-campus work permits). [R87.1(3)(a)]. Officers should verify the work permit information (and any study permit where applicable) in GCMS. If the primary activity is study, then any work done during that period does not qualify for work experience pursuant to R87.1(2).

## Working without a Work Permit

R186 and R187 describe the types of work which a foreign national is authorized to do without having to obtain a work permit. You can refer to the guick reference guide to occupations to ascertain if applicants are exempt from requiring a work permit. Generally speaking, it is possible for work experienced gained under R186 and 187 to apply for CEC, as long as they meet program requirements (1 year in the past 3; NOC 0, A or B; maintain TR status while working). For example, Diplomats, consular officers and other foreign representatives and officials are authorized to work in Canada without a work permit [R186(b) and (c)]. Authorized work within embassies or consulates in Canada could count towards meeting MEC for CEC and obtaining points for CRS as per Ml's, as long as the work is authorized and it meets all other requirements (ie. NOC O, A or B; 1 year in the last 3; language requirements met). Likewise, work experience acquired while under implied status is authorized [R186(u)], and will be considered as eligible work experience under the CEC, provided the applicant continued to work in Canada under the same conditions as their original work permit until a decision was made on their application for a work permit extension.

However, there are exceptions to this and not all work authorized without permit is eligible for the CEC program. For example, R186(a) and R187– Business Visitors: Work experience obtained as a business visitor cannot be calculated for the Canadian experience class (CEC). Business visitors must not have an intent to enter the Canadian labour market (that is, they must have no gainful employment in Canada). Examples: attendance at business meetings, trade conventions or exhibitions; procurement of Canadian goods and services; people seeking entry to repair, service, set up, test or supervise work on specialized commercial or industrial equipment purchased or leased outside Canada; certain foreign nationals in the commercial production industry, such as advertising, or in the film or recording industry, including those using studios (limited to small groups that are renting studios and not entering the labour market).

### Temporary resident status

### Admission to Canada

In addition to meeting the eligibility requirements for the temporary resident category under which they have applied, applicants must obtain either a visa or an electronic travel authorization (if they are visa-exempt), which will allow them to enter Canada. A temporary resident visa (TRV) is an official counterfoil document issued by a visa office that is placed in a person's passport to show that they have met the requirements for admission to Canada as a temporary resident. A TRV does not guarantee entry to Canada (ie. Does not give the “right" of entry), nor does it grant temporary resident status in Canada. The border services officer who examines the foreign national upon entry will determine the purpose and duration of the visit. A handwritten date below the stamp indicates the date by which the foreign national must leave Canada. It is at this point that the foreign national receives temporary resident status. Under IRPA, all foreign

## nationals authorized to enter Canada as per subsection A22(1) have temporary resident status. A temporary

resident may also be authorized to work without a permit [R186], be issued a work permit [R200 or R201], be authorized to study without a permit [R189] or be issued a study permit [R216 or R217].

### Status During Period(s) of Work

It is possible for work permits to be issued to those who may not have status as a temporary resident [R202]. A CEC applicant must have held temporary resident status during the period of work used to meet the CEC Minimum Entry Criteria. A foreign national has temporary resident status when they have been found to meet the requirements of the legislation to enter AND/OR remain in Canada as a visitor, student, worker or temporary resident permit (TRP) holder. Only foreign nationals physically in Canada hold temporary resident status.

Foreign nationals such as refugee claimants in Canada and unauthorized workers or those with expired permits, whose work experience would be accumulated while they have no temporary resident status in Canada, are not eligible for the CEC program. Remarks should indicate that the issuance of a permit does not indicate temporary resident status.

### Working with a Visitor Record

An applicant under the CEC does not need to hold a work permit; they only need to have valid TR status during the qualifying work period(s). In other words, applicants who are authorized to work in Canada under R186 and DO NOT hold a work permit, may still be able to apply under the CEC, but must provide documentation with their application establishing that they had legal temporary status in Canada (e.g., a visitor record for religious workers). A visitor record is a status document issued to both visa-required or visa-exempt foreign nationals. A visitor record may be issued at a POE, to a foreign national seeking to enter Canada, or to one who is already in Canada and wishes to either:

extend their stay in Canada beyond their initial authorized stay;

- restore their status as a temporary resident in Canada, following a loss of their status; or
- change the conditions of their stay

Immigration, Refugees mmigration, Réfugiés and Citizenship Canadaet Citoyenneté Canada L'nformation divulguée en vertu de la toi sur l’accès à Tinformation A visitor record issued to someone who intends to perform authorized work, verifies the status of the temporary resident as work permit exempt and supports their application to Service Canada for their social insurance number. A visitor record issued in this case should include remarks specifying the ability of the foreign national to work without a permit. Acceptable remarks that may appear on the visitor record include: "Work permit exempt as a [job title]”; or "Work permit exempt, per section R186”. A foreign national who holds a valid visitor record with such remarks, authorized to work without a work permit, may be able to include their work to meet CEC minimum entry criteria.

Working with a Temporary Resident Permit

In some cases an officer may issue a TRP to allow a person who is inadmissible, or who does not meet the requirements of the IRPA, to become a temporary resident (that is, to enter or remain in Canada) if it is justified in the circumstances. A temporary resident permit (TRP) confers temporary resident status and as such, applicants who obtained their qualifying work experience while in Canada on a TRP are eligible to apply for the CEC. These applicants are eligible as long as their work in Canada was authorized. Keep in mind that applicants who are inadmissible to Canada cannot be granted permanent residence as members of the CEC. However, this does not preclude the foreign national from applying for permanent residence under the CEC program, nor including work performed while in Canada under a TRP.

The key factor for a reviewing officer to consider is whether the PA held valid temporary resident status during their qualifying work period, as they must meet R186 requirements to be authorized to work pursuant to R87.1(3)(b), and must hold temporary resident status throughout the qualifying period. Holders of temporary resident permits (TRPs) are considered to be in the temporary resident class; however, when a foreign national applies for a new TRP, they are not renewing under R181 but applying for a subsequent TRP. Therefore, they do not maintain their temporary resident status during the processing period as they do not meet the requirements of subsection R183(5). For CEC applicants, any work performed during this period (after the TRP expires, and before the new permit is issued) would not qualify as work experience obtained for the purpose of meeting MEC.

Maintained status during processing (previously called implied status)

A temporary resident may apply to extend their period of authorized stay before it ends. If they have done so, their period of authorized stay as a temporary resident is extended by law until a decision is made [R183(5)]. Such a person is considered to have maintained legal status as a temporary resident during the processing period.

The extension of status by law (maintained status, previously known as implied status) does not automatically authorize a temporary resident to continue working while their application for a renewal of their work permit is in progress. The temporary resident must also meet the requirements of R186(u) to continue working. Paragraph R186(u) applies only until a decision is made on the work permit renewal application.

Section R201 allows foreign nationals to apply for a renewal of their work permit from within Canada, only if the application is made before their present work permit expires. If a temporary resident applies for renewal of their work or study permit before the expiry of their existing permit and their permit expires before a decision is made, paragraph R186(u) or section R189 authorizes them to work or study without a permit under the same conditions pending a determination of their application for renewal and only as long as the person remains in Canada.

Work experience acquired while TR status is maintained will be considered as eligible work experience under CEC, provided the applicant continued to work in Canada under the same conditions as their original work permit until a decision was made on their application for a work permit extension.

Note: TR status is maintained only up until a decision is made on the work permit renewal application. The TR

status expires on the date that a decision is made on the application to extend or renew the original permit. The application may be approved, refused or withdrawn.

Once the original work permit expires, the foreign national cannot submit another application under section R201, because they no longer have a valid work permit. In the 90 days following the expiry of the permit, the foreign national is considered to be without status, but may be able to apply to restore their TR status. However, they no longer meet requirements of paragraph R186(u) because they cannot make the application for restoration while holding a valid permit.

This means that if the foreign national in Canada does not apply to renew their permit prior to its expiry, while they may be eligible for restoration of status, they may not apply to extend or renew the permit AND they are

## no longer authorized to work. Language

In order to meet the MEC for the CEC program, according to R87.1(d) and (e) of the IRPR, at the time of application, an applicant must identify which of English or French is to be considered their first official language and which is to be considered their second official language, and must be assessed by a designated organization and submit the results of that assessment with their application. The applicant must evaluated against the Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB) for English and the Niveaux de compétence linguistique canadien (NCLC) for French, and must achieve minimum scores for reading, writing, speaking and listening. For the CEC program, the applicant must meet minimum language thresholds as follows:

0Canadian Language Benchmark 7 for NOC 0 or A jobs or O Canadian Language Benchmark 5 for NOC B jobs

If an applicant has work experience in both NOC 0 or A as well as NOC B occupations, the applicant must satisfy the officer that they meet the minimum language proficiency threshold for the skill type/level in which they have obtained most (i.e., more than half) of their qualifying work experience [R87.1(2)(e)].

Note: If an applicant has work experience that is split evenly between NOC 0, A or NOC B occupations, the

officer should apply the language proficiency threshold that is most favorable to the applicant.

The following test results are acceptable evidence of language proficiency:

IELTS(International English Language Testing System) administered by the British Council, the University of Cambridge and Education Australia; CELPIP (Canadian English Language Proficiency Index Program), administered by the University of British Columbia; TEF (Test d’évaluation du français) administered by Chambre de commerce de Paris (Alliance Française abroad); and TCF Canada: Test de connaissance du français, administered by Centre international d'études pédagogiques (CIEP) for the French Ministry of Education

Applicants are only required to submit their test reference number. Language test results are verified by CiO clerks at the time of completeness check. Points are awarded based on equivalency grids.

Language test results must be valid (less than two years old) both when the applicant

completes the Express Entry profile; AND applies for permanent residence

##### CRS: Education

There is no education requirement included in the Minimum Entry Criteria for the CEC program. Applicants may be awarded points on the CRS grid for education credentials, and therefore an assessment of education credentials may be required. Applicants must submit either their completed Canadian educational credential or their completed foreign educational credential along with an equivalency assessment (Educational Credential Assessment [ECA] report) issued by a designated assessment organization or CEC 11.2 TRAINING MANUAL APR2021 Page|48 CIO Sydney

Education Credential Assessments (ECA)

Equivalency assessments (ECA reports) will be used as conclusive evidence that the applicant's completed foreign diplomas, certificates or credentials are equivalent to completed Canadian educational credentials. The ECA report will also include an assessment by the organization or institution of the authenticity of the completed foreign diploma, certificate or credential.

If a professional body has been designated for the primary occupation specified in the application, the applicant must submit a completed foreign diploma, certificate or credential relevant to that occupation and the equivalency assessment (ECA report) issued by the designated professional body establishing that the completed foreign diploma, certificate or credential is equivalent to the completed Canadian educational credential required to practice that occupation in at least one of the provinces in which the equivalency assessments issued by this professional body are recognized.

Only reports issued by an IRCC-designated organization or institution will be accepted as an equivalency assessment for the purpose of a federal skilled worker class application.

Applicants are only required to submit their ECA reference number, not a copy of their assessment. ECA reports are verified by CiO clerks at the time of the completeness check. Applicants must declare in their Express Entry profile if they have obtained an ECA for their foreign educational credential. An ECA report must be less than five years old at the time the Express Entry profile is submitted and upon receipt of the application for permanent residence. CRS points are awarded for the highest level of education obtained [EE MI's s. 11(2). Maximum CRS points awarded for education are 150 without a spouse and 140 with a spouse. Points may also be awarded for a spouse's education provided above requirements are met, up to a maximum of 10 points.

ECA reports are only accepted if the report was issued after the organization was designated as an ECA provided for IRCC. There are 7 designated ECA providers as follows:

World Education Services (WES): Date of Designation: April 17, 2013 Comparative Education Service: University of Toronto School of Continuing Studies: Date of Designation: April 17, 2013 International Credential Assessment Service of Canada: Date of Designation: April 17, 2013 Medical Council of Canada: Date of Designation: April 17, 2013 Pharmacy Examining Board of Canada (PEBC): Date of Designation: January 6, 2014 International Credential Evaluation Service (ICES): Date of Designation: August 6, 2015 International Qualifications Assessment Service (IQAS): Date of Designation: August 6, 2015

CRS: Job Offer

A qualifying job offer / offer of arranged employment is defined in subsection 29(2) of the Ministerial Instructions respecting the Express Entry system, and in R82 of the IRPR.

A job offer is considered to be a "qualifying offer of arranged employment" if it is for continuous, paid, full-time work that is, not seasonal, in skill type 0 or skill levels A or B of the National Occupational Classification (NOC) matrix, is for at least one year after issuance of visa for permanent residence, and if it meets one of the following three conditions:

1. the employer making the job offer has a positive Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) from Employment and Social Development Canada that approves the offer and names the candidate and their position; or
2. the candidate
is currently working in Canada in a NOC Skill Type 0 or Skill Level A or B job on a work permit that was issued based on an LMIA, is working for an employer listed on the work permit, is authorized to work in Canada when submitting their application and when the visa is issued, and has received a job offer from their employer for a full-time job in NOC Skill Type 0, A or B for at least one year after becoming a permanent resident; or

3. the candidate has a valid work permit for a job in NOC O, A or B that is exempt from needing an LMIA (under an international agreement such as the North America Free Trade Agreement, a federal-provincial agreement, or other cases supporting Canadian interests) and the candidate (LMIA is exempt work permit under R204 (a) or (c) or R205):
is currently working for an employer specified on the work permit has accumulated one year of full-time work experience (or an equal amount of part-time work) and has a valid job offer from that employer for at least one year after their visa for permanent

## residence is issued.

REMEMBER: The employer must be named on the LMIA-exempt work permit. An ‘open' work permit would not meet this requirement. NOTE: For additional information, refer to the following website:

## GCMS procedures Work through the ADMM and GCMS simultaneously.

EE ELGIBILITY

## 1) Go to Assessment tab and highlight the latest Candidate line.

2) Ensure the CRS score is minimum score or greater and that CEC MEC shows MET.
a) If CEC MEC = NOT MET; refer to the following 11.2 Decision section.
3) Watch for changes in the scores between ITA and REVISED columns.
4) Go to Employment tab; click [W/E Multipull] on ADMM.
## 5) Watch for part-time hours; Canadian employment during full-time study; Self-employment in Canada.

6) Go to Education tab and compare level of education to CRS points in ADMM 7) Watch for Canadian study.
## 8) Go to Job offer tab if CRS points awarded for Arranged Employment.

a) Note the employer; job position; LMIA # if any; Snag-it is helpful at this point.
9) Go to the Language tab to determine the lowest CLB level for the PA. (This is helpful when assessing the Skill Transferability Factors; CLB 7 vs CLB 9) GCMS NOTES
# 10) Go to NOTES view.

11) Review the R10 notes to confirm the language and education documents were verified at R10. CORRESPONDENCE-INCOMING
12) Go to Correspondence-Incoming and sort the items in alphabetical order.
## 13) Review Birth certificates for any children.

14) Review Client Information (or Client Enquiry) for any information relevant to the 11.2 decision.
15) Review the PA's and SP/CLP's Education documents and ensure the CRS points were awarded correctly (compare to ADMM). Note any discrepancies for correction/adjustments later.
16) Review the PA's Employment documents for foreign work experience and any Canadian work to ensure the CRS points were awarded correctly. Toggle on ADMM under CRS Points and other tabs as applicable. Note any discrepancies in ADMM for correction/adjustments later.
17) Review the Funds item to ensure supporting documents are provided. Determine the equivalent in Canadian dollars. If unable to verify the required level of funds, note the eDoc # in ADMM and set the item to “Review Required”. Leave the A11.2 decision as “Review Required" and add an appropriate Summary Note in the ADMM.
## 18) Review any Offer of Employment items, if applicable. Note as applicable in ADMM.

19) Review the Marriage Certificate or Stat Dec of CL Union, if applicable. (Watch for possible marriage of convenience, etc.) Same for divorce certs.
20) Review any other items marked as “Review Required" for any information relevant to the 11.2 decision.
## 21) Review any “Provided” items. Change Status to “Received” & change Review Status as applicable:

## a) Change the Status to "Received".

b) Change the Review Status to:
i) Checked if no further review is required. ii) Review Required if Officer review is required. iii) Assessed if the item was part of your decision.
## 22) Go to [SEARCH]

Scroll down to Person History and review information. Look for the most recent visa (travel visa, work permit, study permit, etc.). Hyperlink into the most recent visa/permit to verify client status. If the client is considered “In Status" – this means the visa applied for is valid as of the application received date. Note client's current status (as per GCMS) into the ADMM. In Status indicates that: The client has an approved application for either worker/visitor/study status in Canada which has not expired OR The client has implied status, i.e. and ongoing permit application applied for prior to the expiry of their previous permit OR The client has restored their status (the client applied for new worker or visitor application during restoration period -90 days following expiry of temporary residence permit) Not in Status indicates that: The client does not have a valid work/visitor/study application, all applications have expired, or been refused. The client has not applied for a new permit within the restoration period (90 days following expiry of temporary residence permit).

### Updating the decision in GCMS

In addition to the 11.2-EE MI decision, since March 2020 agents are now also updating the Selection-EE Econ decision. In the same view as above, once you have entered a decision for A11.2 you will hit New and in the "Type” field choose Selection-EE Econ from the drop-down list. Decisions should be updated according to the following scenarios.

11.2-EE MI = Met Selection-EE Econ = Passed
- No concerns with A11.2 CRS allocations as per the Ministerial Instructions Reserved for situations where the client has provided objective evidence of work experience, including skill level, duties and period of employment. Client has provided evidence of their education and language skills, as applicable. Client has provided sufficient settlement funds, when required.
Note: This status can be used in cases where large deposits may be identified. If the client meets the
 minimum amount for settlement funds, do not reference the large deposit in your A11.2 note as this large deposit should be reviewed from a Security point of view. See below for further instructions.
11.2-EE MI = Met Selection-EE Econ = Recommend Passed •Agents will use their discretion in cases where there are no job duties listed or insufficient job duties are listed on the employment letters but the client has the appropriate education background for that occupation and previous work experience in that field. Also, if the client is currently working in that occupation on a Closed work permit (i.e. primary occupation and employer is listed on work permit), it is very likely that the client's experience was previously assessed during the work permit process and was deemed eligible to work in that field.
- Agent will enter the following in the work experience section of their A1 1.2 note: Letter of employment does not specify main duties of work experience. Based on review of application, including factors such as work permit, education, and work history, I am satisfied PA appears to meet MEC for program
- Officer will review and update the Selection-EE Econ line to Passed, if in agreement.
Note: This status can be used in cases where large deposits may be identified. If the client meets the
 minimum amount for settlement funds, do not reference the large deposit in your A11.2 note as this large deposit should be reviewed from a Security point of view. See below for further instructions.
11.2-EE MI = Not Met [DO NOT GENERATE Selection-EE Econ Line] When client objectively does not meet the A11.2 criteria Further MEC review is not mandatory Do not add the Selection EE-Econ line to GCMS Some general examples when an agent would use this status (list not exhaustive):
Client clearly does not meet the minimum work experience (i.e., less one year in the last 3 yrs) Page | 75CEC 11.2 TRAINING MANUAL APR2021CIO Sydney

Some concerns with program criteria (aka MEC); however these are not minimized by client's previous experience, i.e., age, previous education (field, level), work experience (field, position, skill level), etc. An example would be if a client was educated as a lawyer but they are now working as an accountant.

# Appendix B: Reviewing Work Experience in GCMS

Navigate to the IMM>PR>EE Eligibility>Assessment View. The line with the campaign information is the ITA (Invitation to Apply) record. If there is more than one line with campaign information use the most recent. On this line you will find the CRS score at the time the applicant was invited to apply and the invitation date, as well as the program(s) for which MEC was "Met". The line above this line is the e-APR record. This record contains details of the applicant's application, including the CRS score at the time of application (e-APR). By comparing this with the CRS score at ITA, you can determine whether the score changed between ITA and APR. ## *****A11.2 ASSESSMENT/ R87.1 ELIGIBILITY*****

Response to PFL received. PA submitted letter from employer stating PA worked as an Admin Assis from 05-2021 to 06-2022. PA was hired as Dispatch Assistant from 09-2018 to 12-2018 and was offered the position of Admin Assistant in 05-2021 and she worked until 06-2022. PA also submitted pay stubs and bank statements.

After a careful review of all the information available, I am not satisfied with the explanation submitted in response to PFL. During the call on 20-10-2022, HR Manager was asked about PA' position and duties as Admin Assist specifically during the time from 05-2021 to 06-2022 and she answered that she was a Dispatch Assistant( NOC-C) and never performed the duties of an

#### Admin Assist. In addition, the HR Manager, confirmed this info after looking at the company'

payroll/ software and took her time to review the details.

I am not satisfied the LOEs submitted with the application are credible representations of PA' Canadian work experience and are obtained for the purpose if this application. I am not satisfied PA has acquired Canadian experience as declared but Pa worked with the company for the declared period as a Dispatcher Assist.

I have reviewed all information available, and upon review, I am not satisfied that the PA is a member of the Canadian Experience Class according to R87.1(2).

# Canadian Experience Class (CEC)

The CEC is prescribed as a class of people who are skilled workers with work experience in Canada. The class was developed for temporary foreign workers and foreign graduates with qualifying Canadian work experience who may become permanent residents based on their ability to become economically established in Canada and who intend to reside in a province other than Quebec.

To be eligible, one must:

- Have at least 12 months of full-time skilled work experience in Canada* (or equivalent to 1560 hours), within the last three years before applying.
## MINIMUM

- Have gained work experience** in Canada with the proper authorization
# REQUIREMENTS

### (Temporary resident status)***

- meet the required language levels needed for the job for each language ability (CLB 7 for TEER 0 or 1; CLB 5 for TEER 2 or 3). Test results must be less than 2 years old.
- plan to live outside the province of Quebec (QC has its own programs)

## permanently in Canada

Once in the pool, applicants with the most competitive CRS scores will receive invitations to apply for Canadian permanent residence.

Step 3: Verifying Supporting Documentation on File

Onus is on the applicant to provide sufficient evidence to satisfy the officer that their claimed employment is true. Examples of supporting evidence include: Detailed reference letters, Income tax documents, Educational or Professional transcripts. In cases where the applicant is in a common-law relationship, the officer should review the supporting documentation on file to establish the bona fides of the relationship. You are only required to verify areas where applicant required points for CRS score,

i.e. if the 50 points for foreign employment is not required for them to meet the minimum entry score for the campaign date you do not need to assess the foreign work experience. All letter of employment (LOE) should include: an official document printed on company letterhead must include applicant's name company's contact information name, title and signature of the immediate supervisor etc. indicate all positions held while employed at the company current job title duties and responsibilities job status (if current job) dates worked for the company number of work hours per week annual salary (plus benefits)

## Refusals under EE Eligibility

Officers should refuse an application under section A11.2 if it is determined that at the time of the ITA or e-APR, the applicant did not or does not meet the MEC, which includes the requirements of the program to which they were invited to apply; or the applicant's recalculated CRS score has fallen below that of the lowest-ranked candidate invited to apply in that round of invitations.

# Glossary

Applicant-A person who has filled out and submitted a complete application for permanent residence.

### ADMM – Assisted Decision Making Macro Computer software developed by Gaston Gaulin and

other IRCC workers to streamline case analyst and assistant processing of economic immigration applications.

## ARC – Authorization to Return to Canada. Foreign nationals subject to an enforced removal

order may not return to Canada without authorization from an officer.

## Canadian educational credential means any secondary school diploma or any post-secondary

diploma, certificate or credential that is issued on the completion of a Canadian program of study or training at an educational or training institution that is recognized by the provincial

### authorities responsible for registering, accrediting, supervising and regulating such institutions.

(diplôme canadien)

### CAIPS – Computer Assisted Immigration Processing System. CAIPS was a precursor to our

current GCMS. Canadian Experience Class (CEC) - is prescribed as a class of persons who may become permanent residents on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada, their experience in Canada, and their intention to reside in a province other than the Province of Quebec.

## CELPIP-Canadian English Language Proficiency Index Program. A private-sector English

## language testing organization from which IRCC accepts tests from applicants for the FSW and

other immigration classes. CLB-Canadian Language Benchmarks means, for the English language, the Canadian Language Benchmarks: English as a Second Language for Adults developed by the Centre for Canadian Language Benchmarks, as amended from time to time. (Canadian Language Benchmarks) Candidate-This term should be used in relation to Express Entry / profile / submission. It refers to a person in the Express Entry pool. Candidates in the pool are ranked against others in the pool. Employers with a Labour Market Impact Assessment may hire Express Entry candidates

## Clo – Centralized Intake Office (in Sidney, Nova Scotia). They received new FSW applications,

triage cases to either IR or the CPC-O, ensure the applications are complete (R10), verify

### education credentials and take the criminality decisions on our files.

CoPR – Confirmation of Permanent Residence is a document issued by IRCC to prospective immigrants upon the approval of an application for permanent residence. It contains biographical information and a passport photograph, and must be presented by the immigrant, along with their passport at a point of entry in order to complete the processing towards permanent residency.

### CRS – The Comprehensive Ranking System, or CRS, determines a candidate's position in the

Express Entry pool. It ranks prospective skilled immigrants by looking at their skills, work experience, language ability, education and other factors that we know lead to success in Canada.

Dependent child, in respect of a parent, means a child who

a. has one of the following relationships with the parent, namely,
i. is the biological child of the parent, if the child has not been adopted by a
person other than the spouse or common-law partner of the parent, or

i. is the adopted child of the parent; and
b. is in one of the following situations of dependency, namely
i. is less than 19 years of age and is not a spouse or common-law partner, or ii. is 19 years of age or older and has depended substantially on the financial
support of the parent since before the age of 19 and is unable to be financially self- supporting due to a physical or mental condition. EA – Employment Authorization ECA – An Educational Credential Assessment, or ECA, is a report issued by an organization designated by the Minister (such as such as CELPIP, IELTS, TEF) that verifies the authenticity of a foreign diploma, certificate or credential, and assesses its equivalence to a Canadian educational credential. EE – Express Entry ESDC – Employment and Social Development Canada FST Federal Skilled Trades Class (sometimes MST) is prescribed as a class of persons who are skilled trades workers and who may become permanent residents on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada in a skilled trade occupation and their intention to reside in a province other than the Province of Quebec. Federal Skilled Workers (FSW) - the federal skilled worker class is hereby prescribed as a class of persons who are skilled workers and who may become permanent residents on the basis of their ability to become economically established in Canada and who intend to reside in a province other than the Province of Quebec. Foss – Field Operations Support System Foreign National-a person who is not a Canadian citizen or a permanent resident, and includes a stateless person. (étranger) Full-time work-Pursuant to R73(1), "full-time work" means at least 30 hours of work over a period of one week, and pursuant to R73(2), "work” means an activity for which wages are paid or commission is earned. GCMS – Global Case Management System IELTS-International English Language Testing System IRCC – Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada facilitates the arrival of immigrants, provides protection to refugees, and offers programming to help newcomers settle in Canada. It also grants citizenship, issues travel documents (such as passports) to Canadians and promotes multiculturalism. Invitation to Apply (ITA) - An Invitation to Apply, or ITA, is given to Express Entry candidates who have the highest Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) scores at the time of an Express Entry round of invitations. Those who receive an ITA have 90 days to apply. This deadline is indicated in the client's correspondence, which they can access in their MyCiC account. Candidates who are issued an

ITA have three options: they can respond to the ITA; they can ignore it (in which case they are removed from the Express Entry pool); they can decline it, in which case they return to the pool for consideration in future rounds of invitations. LMIA – Labour Market Impact Assessment. An LMIA is a document issued by Employment and Social Development Canada which gives permission to an employer to hire certain types of foreign workers. A positive LMIA attests that there is a need for workers but there are no Canadians available to do it. Noc – National Occupational Classification is the official governmental classification and

# description of occupations in the Canadian economy. The NOC identifies and groups

occupations in the Canadian economy by skill type and level based on the tasks, duties and responsibilities of the occupation. PA – Principal Applicant-A person who has filled out and submitted a complete application for permanent residence. (Same as Applicant).

# PR – Permanent Resident means a person who has acquired permanent resident status and has

not subsequently lost that status under section 46. (résident permanent) Round of invitations-A round of invitations occurs on a specific time and day when IRCC issues Invitations to Apply to the top-ranking candidates in the Express Entry pool. A round of invitations can be performed for the pool as a whole (Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) rank only) or specific to a program (CRS rank for federal skilled worker only). Skilled Trade occupation-Pursuant to R87.2(1), a "skilled trade occupation" is defined as an occupation in one of the following categories belonging to Skill Level B of the NOC, unless the occupation has been designated a restricted occupation by the Minister: •Major Group 72, industrial, electrical and construction trades; •Major Group 73, maintenance and equipment operation trades;

# •Major Group 82, supervisors and technical occupations in natural resources, agriculture

and related production; •Major Group 92, processing, manufacturing and utilities supervisors and central control operators; •Minor Group 632, chefs and cooks; and •Minor Group 633, butchers and bakers. SP – Study Permit means a written authorization to engage in academic, professional,

vocational or other education or training in Canada that is issued by an officer to a foreign national. (permis d’études)

Good morning everyone, As discussed in yesterday's email, we will be sending out information on all LOBs regarding the change

from NOC 2016 to NOC 2021: the following will cover Canadian Experience Class, Federal Skilled Worker and Federal Skilled Trades. The preliminary PDI's for these programs have been attached, and will be published on November 16th 2022 following the NOC 2021 implementation. Below, I have provided all of the changes contained in the PDIs which will affect processing of applications received on or after November 16th 2022. Applications received before November 16th 2022 will still be processed using NOC 2016 codes and job descriptions. For Express Entry, communication is updated on the client side and push notifications are being sent regularly to clients to use Noc 2021 codes. All clients currently in a pool must change their profile to adhere to the NOC 2021 structure and will only receive an ITA after this is complete. More than happy to schedule meetings on MsTeams to go through the information, or if you have questions or concerns; you can send me an e-mail or a direct message on MsTeams!

As an overview, the implementation of the new NOC 2021 TEER structure entails 2 factors: The structure from NOC 2016 (NOC 0, A, B, C and D) will be replaced with a 6-category TEER system 4 digit codes are replaced by 5 digit codes Skill type or level (NOC 2016) TEER category (NOC 2021)

## Skill type 0 TEER O

## Skill level A TEER 1

Skill level B TEER 2 and TEER 3

## Skill level CTEER 4

## Skill level D TEER 5

A-2025-58066-000665

For Express Entry, this means that occupations in TEERs 0, 1, 2, 3 are eligible to meet program requirements, previously structured as NOC 0, A, B.

- The majority of NOCs that were eligible under the previous NOC 2016 Skill type or level 0, A, B, are still eligible under the NOC 2021 TEERs 0,1,2,3 although they may changed the category they now fall under (a Skill A NOC may now be under TEER 2), and some NOC 2016 NOCs have been split under NOC 2021 to specify job titles:
# For example: 0112 - Human resources managers (NOC 2016)

is now split into 5 10011 – Human resources mangers (NOC 2021) 11200 – Human resources professionals (NOC 2021) 13110 – Administrative Assistants (NOC 2021)

# 21120 – Public and environmental health and safety professionals (NOC 2021)

22232 – Occupational health and safety specialist (NOC 2021)

- ESDC has provided the following updated pages to help during the transition. It is recommended to search for the provided NOC code for every application as staff adjust to the new structure and 5 digit codes Find your job: National Occupational Classification 2021 - Canada.ca Concordance Table: NOC concordance tables-Canada.ca (esdc.gc.ca) (table comparing all NOC 2106 to 2021 codes)
### New Eligible/Ineligible NOCs

Certain occupations which were ineligible under NOC 2016, are now eligible under NOC 2021. The following list only applies to applications received on and after November 16th 2022. Applications received before November 16th 2022 with the following occupations are still ineligible.

Payroll administrators – NOC 13102 Dental assistants and dental laboratory assistants – NOC 33100 Nurse aides, orderlies and patient service associates-NOC 33102 Pharmacy technical assistants and pharmacy assistants – NOC 33103 Elementary and secondary school teacher assistants – NOC 43100 Sheriffs and bailiffs – NOC 43200 Correctional service officers – NOC 43201 By-law enforcement and other regulatory officers – NOC 43202 Estheticians, electrologists and related occupations – NOC 63211 Residential and commercial installers and servicers – NOC 73200 Pest controllers and fumigators – NOC 73202 Transport truck drivers – NOC 73300 Bus drivers, subway operators and other transit operators – NOC 73301 Heavy equipment operators – NOC 73400 Aircraft assemblers and aircraft assembly inspectors – NOC 93200
